This is not a P/E-vs-EV/EBITDA restatement — a single year's EBITDA does not determine both answers. Their overlap (Rs 237-291) is honest corroboration rather than arithmetic, and neither leg comes close to the traded price.
EXIDEIND.rationale: Exide is a mature lead-acid battery duopolist whose accounting has gone nowhere while the balance sheet has ballooned: revenue grew from Rs 15,078 cr to 17,995 cr (4.4% in FY26, decelerating), EBITDA margin sat flat at 10.4-10.9%, and PAT went 823 to 883 to 801 to 860 cr — so consolidated ROE fell to 6.2% on net worth of Rs 13,905 cr as capex of Rs 5,973 cr over four years (2.7x depreciation) went into a pre-revenue lithium-ion gigafactory. The normalised-earnings leg gives Rs 237-342/share (core at 13-18x ~Rs 1,000 cr of core PAT, plus Rs 4,900-5,400 cr of net financial assets and Rs 3,000-5,000 cr for the lithium venture at roughly invested cost); the owner-cash-flow leg gives Rs 209-291/share (core owner earnings of Rs 750-900 cr capitalised at 13.3-16.7x, plus the same non-core assets). I would defend Rs 240-290, which puts the core on 11.8-15.7x and the whole company on 1.5-1.8x book — fair for a 4-6% grower with pass-through pricing on lead and a structurally poor cash conversion record. At Rs 449.80 the market is paying 44.8x reported earnings and 2.77x book, which requires the unproven lithium business to be worth Rs 15,000 cr-plus today; that is an option I will not underwrite at 55% above my band top, so AVOID — with the honest caveat that the lithium venture is the single largest swing factor and a credible bull case pushes my ceiling toward Rs 330, still well short of the price.

FEDFINA.method_1: Peer-relative P/E on normalised earnings (EPS Rs 8.28–9.50 after topping loan-loss coverage from 25% toward 40%, x 12–15x for a 12.6%-ROE, ~20%-growth, 86%-secured retail NBFC) → Rs 99–142
FEDFINA.method_2: Residual income / justified P/B on tangible book (TBVPS Rs 77.66; ROE ramp 12.6%→15–16.5% as leverage rebuilds from 5.77x toward 6.5x; CoE 12.5–14%, terminal g 5–7%; stressed-book floor Rs 71.9) → Rs 85–135, i.e. 1.1–1.75x book
FEDFINA.methods_are_independent: They are linked only by the identity P/B = ROE x P/E, and that identity is exactly where they pull apart here rather than agreeing. Leg 1 takes a single realised year's earnings and prices it off what the market pays for comparable Indian secured-retail NBFCs; it never sees a cost of equity, a terminal growth rate, or the balance sheet. Leg 2 ignores the peer tape entirely: it starts from tangible book and credits value ONLY for ROE earned above an explicitly derived CoE along a multi-year path, so its answer is driven by three inputs (CoE 12.5–14%, terminal g 5–7%, ROE trajectory 12.6%→16.5%) that Leg 1 has no view on. The wedge is real and it is directional: FY26 ROE of 12.6% sits BELOW the sustainable ROE that a 12–15x P/E implicitly assumes, so the earnings leg lands higher (Rs 99–142) than the book leg (Rs 85–135) and their midpoints sit 12% apart (Rs 121 vs Rs 108) — if these were one method restated they would coincide at both ends, as they would if I had paired P/E with EV/EBITDA. Leg 2 also performs a solvency test (25% PCR, full-NNPA write-off to BVPS 71.9) that no earnings multiple can perform, and Leg 1 performs a provisioning normalisation that the book leg takes as given. Note that for an NBFC there is no honest cash-flow leg: operating cash flow is structurally negative (FY26 -Rs 1,664 cr) because loan growth is an operating outflow, so "FCF" here measures balance-sheet expansion, not distributable cash, and was correctly excluded.
FEDFINA.rationale: Fedbank Financial Services is a sub-scale but genuinely compounding secured-retail NBFC: AUM Rs 14,500 cr, 24% PAT CAGR over FY23–26 (Rs 180 cr → Rs 344 cr), NIM 8%, ROA 2.28%, GNPA 2.0%/NNPA 1.5%, CRAR 20.5%, and a real FY26 efficiency inflection (opex fell in absolute terms from Rs 873 cr to Rs 832 cr while NII grew 14%, taking cost/income from 73.8% to 61.9%). The problem is that all of this still only produces a 12.6% ROE on Rs 2,926 cr of net worth, because post-IPO leverage of 5.77x assets/equity is below the 6.69x it ran at in FY23. The earnings leg (normalised EPS 8.3–9.5 x 12–15x) gives Rs 99–142; the residual-income leg on tangible book (CoE 12.5–14%, ROE ramping to 15–16.5%) gives Rs 85–135 or 1.1–1.75x book; I would defend Rs 102–132, midpoint Rs 117 (~1.5x book, ~13x normalised earnings). At Rs 153.83 the stock trades at 1.98x book and 16.9x trailing, which by the Gordon identity requires terminal ROE of ~16.5% AND a 12.5% CoE AND 8.4% perpetual growth simultaneously — a triple-optimistic reading of a lender whose coverage ratio is 25% and whose ROE has not yet exceeded 13.6% in any year on record. The ROE-expansion story is credible but is already more than fully paid for; hence REDUCE, not AVOID.

FINCABLES.method_1: Sum-of-parts on ACCRUAL EARNINGS: core wires-and-cables operation valued on post-tax operating earnings (EBIT x (1-23.1% eff tax) = Rs 410-431 cr, using 3-yr avg EBIT 533.6 to FY26's 560.1) at 15-20x, plus the treasury (net cash Rs 2,031 cr at 82-92%, non-current investments Rs 2,462 cr at 60-78% for illiquidity/strategic-stake/tax). Gives Rs 9,298-12,403 cr equity = Rs 608-811/sh.
FINCABLES.method_2: Owner CASH FLOW: core NOPAT Rs 430.7 cr with reinvestment set by the capital the business actually consumes (44 paise of working capital per rupee of incremental sales, FY24-26), capitalised two-stage. No-growth case (marginal capital earns only WACC) Rs 3,589 cr; g=6%/ROIC 15%/WACC 12% Rs 4,307 cr; generous g=8%/ROIC 18%/WACC 11.5% Rs 6,837 cr. Plus the same discounted treasury = Rs 440-694/sh.
FINCABLES.methods_are_independent: Leg 1 keys off accrual EBIT and the carrying value of assets; Leg 2 keys off cash actually left after the working capital and capex the business consumes. For most companies they converge; here they cannot, and the gap is the whole story. Four-year cash conversion is 46% (avg OCF Rs 297 cr vs avg PAT Rs 643 cr), and FY26 posted record PAT of Rs 714 cr alongside OCF of Rs 49 cr and FCF of MINUS Rs 105 cr. They also disagree on growth's worth: Leg 1's multiple implicitly rewards 12.2% revenue CAGR, while Leg 2 penalises it because the Rs 921 cr of incremental capital employed FY23-26 produced only Rs 97 cr of incremental EBIT — a 10.5% pre-tax (~8% post-tax) incremental return, below cost of capital. If the FY25-26 inventory build is a one-off copper-stocking cycle the legs converge near Rs 700; if 44% incremental WC intensity is structural, Leg 2 is right and the earnings multiple is unearned. That is a genuine ~Rs 250/sh disagreement, not arithmetic.
FINCABLES.rationale: Finolex Cables is a #3 branded wires-and-cables manufacturer with a good core business buried under an idle balance sheet. Revenue grew 12.2% CAGR to Rs 6,321 cr (FY26 +18.8%) but EBITDA margin fell from 11.4% to 9.8% and EBIT compounded only 6.5%, so the top-line growth is largely copper pass-through against rising competitive intensity; core capital employed of ~Rs 2,000 cr earns 28% pre-tax ROCE in aggregate, yet incremental capital FY23-26 earned just 10.5% pre-tax. Roughly 40% of the Rs 714 cr PAT (Rs 283 cr post-tax) is non-operating treasury and associate income, so headline EPS of 46.7 and 21.2x P/E flatter the operating business; reported ROE is only 12.3% against a 2.48x P/B because Rs 4,493 cr of cash and investments sit undeployed on a 17% dividend payout. Leg 1 (core post-tax earnings Rs 410-431 cr at 15-20x plus discounted treasury) gives Rs 608-811/sh; Leg 2 (owner FCF on observed reinvestment intensity) gives Rs 440-694/sh, and the intersection is Rs 608-694. My defended band is Rs 610-760, extending the top only to allow the FY25-26 working-capital build to reverse; at Rs 760 the market pays 12.7x core EBIT plus full discounted treasury, which is fair for a margin-compressing category. At Rs 987.6 the market is paying 18.9x core EBIT with full credit for cash that has not been deployed or returned in years — roughly 30% above my top, hence REDUCE rather than AVOID, since the business is debt-free, brand-led and structurally sound.

GALLANTT.method_1: Normalised-earnings multiple. FY26 EBITDA margin of 16.2% is above mid-cycle for a long-steel producer; normalising to 14-15.5% on ~Rs4,600cr revenue gives EBITDA Rs645-715cr, less D&A Rs140cr, plus ~Rs55cr other income on the net cash, less Rs45cr interest = PBT Rs515-585cr; at a normalised 24% tax rate (FY26's 19.8% is a one-off vs FY25's 29.5%) PAT is Rs391-445cr. Applying 13-17x — the upper half of the Indian integrated long-steel peer band, credited for net cash, mid-teens ROIC and a real cost-curve advantage — gives equity value Rs5,083-7,565cr, i.e. Rs211-313 per share on 24.13cr shares.
GALLANTT.method_2: Owner-earnings / FCF yield. Normalised operating cash flow at the historical 0.84 conversion off mid-cycle EBITDA is Rs542-600cr; maintenance capex is Rs150-180cr (1.2-1.4x the Rs130cr D&A on a Rs2,126cr gross-PPE steel plant), well below the Rs348cr actually being spent on expansion. Owner earnings therefore Rs362-450cr. Capitalised at a 7-9% required free-cash yield for a small-cap Indian commodity cyclical, plus Rs285cr net cash, gives Rs4,307-6,714cr equity, i.e. Rs178-278 per share.
GALLANTT.methods_are_independent: They diverge because the company is mid-capex-ramp and its cash economics differ sharply from its accounting earnings. Leg 1 asks what the plant earns at a mid-cycle margin and prices that stream on a peer multiple; its answer is driven by my margin-normalisation choice and by peer multiples. Leg 2 asks what the business would hand an owner if it stopped growing — it deliberately ignores reported PAT, adds back the Rs130cr D&A charge, and instead charges only the Rs150-180cr of true replacement capex against the Rs348cr the company is actually spending; its answer is driven by cash conversion, working-capital behaviour and the required yield. The two legs move in opposite directions on the same facts: OCF/PAT of 1.24 pushes the cash leg up, while charging real maintenance capex and demanding a cyclical's 7-9% yield pushes it down, and neither effect appears in the earnings leg at all. In the event the cash leg landed roughly Rs30/share BELOW the earnings leg at both ends rather than tracking it, which is the sign they are not one method restated. A P/B cross-check on sustainable ROE (1.3-2.0x book = Rs183-275) was used only to confirm, not as a third leg.
GALLANTT.rationale: Leg 1 (normalised PAT Rs391-445cr at 13-17x) gives Rs211-313; leg 2 (owner earnings Rs362-450cr at a 7-9% yield plus Rs285cr net cash) gives Rs178-278; the intersection is roughly Rs211-278, which I widen modestly to Rs205-285 for genuine steel-cycle uncertainty. The business is a genuinely improved regional integrated long-steel maker — EBITDA margin tripled from 8.6% to 16.2% on ~Rs550cr of growth capex, receivables run 15 days, and it carries Rs285cr net cash — but revenue has been essentially flat at ~Rs4,300-4,400cr, so all the gain is cost-curve rather than volume, and cost-curve advantages in commodities get competed away as peers integrate. At Rs614.6 the market is paying 30.6x trailing PAT and 20.3x EV/EBITDA for a business earning ~15% ROE on a Rs3,316cr book; even an aggressive build-out case (capex-funded doubling of the asset base to ~Rs850cr PAT by FY30, capitalised at 15x and discounted four years at 13%) reaches only ~Rs324/share, and at 20x only ~Rs432. I cannot construct a defensible path to the current price, so the call is AVOID with roughly 55-65% downside to my band.

HBLENGINE.method_1: Normalised-earnings multiple. Normalised PAT Rs 750-850 cr (revenue Rs 3,600-4,200 cr at 26-29% EBITDA margin, i.e. FY26's 32.8% peak margin fades but rollout volume grows, leaving FY26's Rs 798 cr PAT roughly as the sustainable level). Multiple 18-26x, built as a blend of a Kavach railway-signalling franchise multiple (28-32x for RDSO-certified, safety-critical, high-ROIC electronics) and the legacy industrial-battery half (12-15x, competitive and commodity-like), then haircut for monopsony customer risk (Indian Railways is effectively the only buyer), tender-driven margin mean-reversion as more Kavach vendors get certified, and Rs 646 cr of government receivables (71 days). No net-cash add-back, since other income on the Rs 726 cr cash pile is already inside PAT. Range Rs 13,500-22,100 cr equity = Rs 495-815/sh, centre ~Rs 648.
HBLENGINE.method_2: Explicit-fade DCF on owner cash flow. Base FCF Rs 580-680 cr (FY26 OCF Rs 738 cr less capex Rs 150 cr = Rs 588 cr; upper end normalises the working-capital drag of a +68% revenue year). Path: 12-18% FCF growth for years 1-5 as the Kavach national rollout peaks, 8-10% for years 6-10, 5% terminal; CoE 13.0-13.5% (risk-free ~6.8%, ERP ~6%, beta ~1.1-1.2, net cash so WACC = CoE); plus Rs 660 cr net cash. Base case gives EV ~Rs 12,700-13,000 cr and equity ~Rs 13,300-13,600 cr = Rs 490-500/sh; bull path (18% then 10%) Rs 540-650/sh; steep-fade bear (post-peak air pocket in year 4, 4% terminal) Rs 250-300/sh. Defensible range Rs 400-620/sh.
HBLENGINE.methods_are_independent: They are not restatements of each other because they answer different questions and are driven by different inputs. Leg 1 prices a profit LEVEL against comparable multiples and is completely indifferent to duration — it never states how long the Kavach economics last. Leg 2 prices the DURATION of the cash-flow runway with an explicit growth-and-fade path and is indifferent to what peers trade at. They can and did diverge sharply: Leg 1 centres on Rs 648 while Leg 2's base case is ~Rs 500, a 30% gap, because a 24x multiple silently embeds roughly 9-10% perpetual growth at a 13.5% CoE, whereas the DCF forces that growth to be a stated, falsifiable input. The legs are also not arithmetically locked at the cash level: unlike a P/E-vs-EV/EBITDA pair (where PAT is a fixed function of EBITDA once interest, D&A and tax are set), FCF here is genuinely decoupled from PAT — capex runs ~3x depreciation (Rs 150 cr vs Rs 51 cr) and working capital against a government customer swings violently, so FCF/PAT was 45% in FY25 (Rs 117 cr on Rs 263 cr) versus 74% in FY26 (Rs 588 cr on Rs 798 cr). A year of heavy receivable build would move Leg 2 hard while leaving Leg 1 untouched.
HBLENGINE.rationale: HBL is a genuinely high-quality asset-light franchise mid-transformation: FY26 revenue Rs 3,303 cr (+68%), EBITDA margin 32.8% versus 19.9% in FY25 and 10.8% in FY23, PAT Rs 798 cr (3x FY25), ~43% ROE, ~60% post-tax ROIC on ~Rs 1,220 cr operating capital, Rs 660 cr net cash and zero leverage — the Kavach/TCAS railway-signalling mix displacing low-margin industrial batteries. The caution is that FY25 revenue actually FELL versus FY24 (Rs 1,967 cr vs Rs 2,233 cr), which is hard evidence that this is lumpy, tender-driven revenue from a single monopsony customer, so FY26's profit level must be normalised rather than extrapolated, and margin mean-reversion is near-certain as more vendors clear RDSO certification. My earnings leg (18-26x on normalised PAT of Rs 750-850 cr) gives Rs 495-815 and my fade-DCF leg (FCF base Rs 580-680 cr, 12-18% then 8-10% growth, 5% terminal, 13-13.5% CoE, plus net cash) gives Rs 400-620; the intersection is Rs 490-630, centred ~Rs 560. At Rs 718.7 the market is paying 24.4x normalised PAT, 17.4x EV/EBITDA and a 3.0% FCF yield — roughly 14% above my band top, so the price already discounts the Kavach runway persisting at FY26 economics for a decade, which the FY25 revenue decline says is not yet proven. Verdict REDUCE: good business, price ahead of defensible value; a confirmed multi-year order book at FY26 margins would move me back to HOLD.

HOMEFIRST.method_1: Forward earnings multiple: FY27E EPS ~64-67 (FY26 EPS 51.61 grown ~24-28% on a fully-deployed post-raise book) at 16-22x, a band set by a 20%+ EPS compounder with ~4% ROA but decelerating AUM growth and rising bank competition in home loans. Range Rs 1,020-1,420.
HOMEFIRST.method_2: Balance-sheet / sustainable-ROE anchor: 10-year residual-income model off FY26 book of Rs 4,356.5 cr (BVPS 416.1), CoE 12.5-13%, ROE path rising from 15.4% to a steady-state 16.6-18.5% (ROA 3.6-3.9% x normalised leverage ~5x), terminal RI growth 5-7%; cross-checked with justified P/B = (ROE-g)/(CoE-g) at 1.7-3.1x. Range Rs 850-1,090, i.e. 2.05-2.62x book.
HOMEFIRST.methods_are_independent: They key off denominators that just moved in opposite directions. The FY26 equity raise added ~Rs 1,333 cr (net worth 2,521 -> 4,357, only ~502 cr from retained earnings), so book jumped 73% while PAT grew 41% — leverage fell 4.84x to 3.48x and closing-book ROE is 12.4% versus 15.7% on average book. The P/E leg prices the near-term earnings stream and needs no view on terminal ROE or cost of equity; the P/B/RI leg is driven almost entirely by whether steady-state ROE exceeds CoE and by terminal growth, and treats the undeployed fresh capital as a drag rather than as earnings. Empirically they did diverge: midpoints Rs ~1,220 versus Rs ~950, a 25% gap, with only a sliver of literal overlap. Had the fresh capital not been raised, or had I used EV/EBITDA off the same PL, the two would have been arithmetic restatements — here they are answering different questions (growth runway versus capital productivity).
HOMEFIRST.rationale: Home First is a genuinely good affordable-housing lender: FY26 revenue Rs 1,753 cr, PAT Rs 540 cr (+41%), ROA 3.95%, cost/income down to 30.2%, credit cost just 0.45% of average assets, and assets compounding 24-41%. Leg A (FY27E EPS 64-67 x 16-22x) gives Rs 1,020-1,420; Leg B (residual income on BVPS 416 at CoE 12.5-13%, steady ROE 16.6-18.5%, terminal g 5-7%, equivalently 2.05-2.62x book) gives Rs 850-1,090. The gap is real: the Rs 1,333 cr raise leaves the balance sheet under-levered at 3.48x, so the ROE-anchored leg penalises capital that is not yet earning, while the earnings leg assumes it gets deployed at ~18-19% incremental returns. I weight the balance-sheet leg slightly higher because that is the discipline that catches over-valued lenders, and I dock the earnings leg for two visible risks — a 0.45% credit cost that is below any through-cycle norm, and an FY26 spread that looks cyclically peak (interest expense grew only 5% while borrowings grew 11%). Band Rs 950-1,200 (2.3-2.9x book, 18-23x FY26 earnings); at Rs 1,189 the stock sits at the very top edge — fully valued, not mispriced.

HONAUT.method_1: Normalised operating-earnings multiple, sum-of-parts: normalised EBIT margin 11.5-13.0% on FY26 revenue of Rs 4,682 cr -> EBIT Rs 538-609 cr, taxed at the observed 25.9% -> NOPAT Rs 399-451 cr, capitalised at 28-38x (justified by >50% ROIC on operating capital, negative working capital, MNC governance, but only 5% EBIT CAGR and a 4-year gross-margin slide), plus net cash of Rs 3,695 cr valued at an 85-95% haircut for the 18% payout / idle-cash drag. Gives Rs 16,250-23,450 per share.
HONAUT.method_2: Two-stage FCFF DCF on core operating cash flow: normalised core FCF of Rs 410-460 cr (OCF Rs 493 cr less capex normalised up toward D&A at Rs 45-54 cr vs the Rs 28-33 cr actually spent; 4-year reported FCF average Rs 412 cr corroborates), grown 5%/8%/11% for 10 years at a WACC of 12.0%/11.5%/11.0% with terminal growth 4.0%/5.0%/5.5%, plus the same haircut net cash. Gives Rs 10,070 (bear) / Rs 13,750 (base) / Rs 19,240 (bull).
HONAUT.methods_are_independent: They genuinely diverged - leg-1 centre Rs 19,850 vs leg-2 centre Rs 13,750, a 44% gap - and the overlap is only Rs 16,250-19,250, so this is corroboration by argument, not by arithmetic. Structurally: (a) leg 2 is NOT a rescaling of leg 1 because cash conversion here is ~115% of NOPAT, not 100% - capex runs at 60% of D&A (Rs 33 cr vs Rs 54 cr) and net working capital is structurally NEGATIVE and getting more so (-58.6 -> -92.8 -> -100.7 -> -187.1 Rs cr across FY23-26, i.e. suppliers and customer advances fund growth), so the earnings-to-cash bridge is a real judgement with a two-way error, not a constant; (b) the two legs are driven by different unknowns - leg 1 turns on whether the gross-margin slide from 46.5% to 38.2% reverses (a mix/pricing question), leg 2 turns on r minus g and on whether sub-D&A capex is sustainable (a duration/discount-rate question). Set the margin normalisation wrong and only leg 1 moves; set terminal growth wrong and only leg 2 moves. I deliberately did NOT use P/E against EV/EBITDA, which for this company are mechanically the same statement.
HONAUT.rationale: Honeywell Automation India is a genuinely high-quality, asset-light industrial-automation franchise - core ROIC of 52% on just Rs 768 cr of operating equity (net worth Rs 4,463 cr less Rs 3,695 cr net cash), negative working capital, capex of only Rs 33 cr against Rs 54 cr of depreciation - but it is not compounding: revenue grew at a 10.7% CAGR over FY23-26 while EBIT grew only 5.1%, because gross margin fell from 46.5% to 38.2% and EBITDA margin from 15.1% to 12.7%, and roughly Rs 168 cr of the Rs 525 cr reported FY26 PAT is interest income on the cash pile rather than operating profit. The earnings leg (NOPAT Rs 399-451 cr at 28-38x plus haircut net cash) gives Rs 16,250-23,450; the cash-flow leg (normalised core FCF Rs 410-460 cr, two-stage DCF at 11.0-12.0% WACC) gives Rs 10,070-19,240 - the DCF is the more sceptical because it will not pay for growth the company has not converted into profit. I would defend Rs 14,500-20,500, which still concedes 24-34x earnings and 17-27x EV/EBIT to a mid-single-digit grower. At Rs 38,155 the stock trades at 64x earnings, 50x EV/EBITDA and a 1.5% core FCF yield; even assuming a full snap-back to the FY23 peak 15% EBITDA margin, the price demands 57x recovered operating NOPAT, so the AVOID does not depend on my margin view being right.

HUDCO.method_1: Normalised-earnings multiple: PAT rebuilt from PPOP with a 25% tax rate (reversing the FY26 -Rs813cr tax credit) and mid-cycle provisions, capitalised at a peer-set P/E of 9.5-12.5x for a PSU infrastructure spread lender.
HUDCO.method_2: Two-stage residual-income / justified P/B on book: B0 Rs21,975cr with 10 years of (ROE - CoE) excess return plus a half-fade perpetuity, ROE 13.5-16%, CoE 12-14%, growth funded only by retained earnings (g = ROE x retention ~9.4%).
HUDCO.methods_are_independent: They are not restatements of each other because neither input drives the other. Leg 1's multiple is set exogenously by what the market pays a rupee of PSU-lender earnings (peer comparables); it is wholly insensitive to cost of equity and, critically, charges nothing for the equity capital HUDCO must retain to fund 20-30% book growth - so it rewards the growth. Leg 2 ignores market multiples entirely and asks only whether ROE exceeds CoE and by how much, explicitly debiting the capital that growth consumes; with a sustainable ROE of ~14.5% against a ~13% CoE the excess spread is barely 1.5 points, so it caps value near 1.2-1.3x book regardless of how fast the book compounds. The two legs therefore encode opposite views of the same fact: Leg 1 says 27% asset growth is worth paying for, Leg 2 says growth at a return equal to the hurdle rate creates zero value. They duly disagreed - Leg 1 gave Rs133-186 (centre ~158) and Leg 2 gave Rs105-160 (centre ~128), a 23% gap between centres, with only partial overlap. Had sustainable ROE been 20%+ they would have converged; at 14% they cannot, and the divergence is real information rather than arithmetic.
HUDCO.rationale: HUDCO is a leveraged, government-owned spread lender whose 30% balance-sheet growth is producing no pre-tax profit growth: FY26 PBT FELL to Rs3,221cr from Rs3,637cr despite interest income rising 27%, because NII/avg assets compressed 3.29% to 2.86% and the provision line swung to +Rs836cr from write-backs of -Rs183cr/-Rs282cr in FY24/FY25. Reported EPS of Rs20.15 (9.7x, ROE 20.2%) is an illusion created by a negative Rs813cr tax line versus a 25.5-25.7% effective rate in every prior year; normalising tax to 25% and provisions to Rs100-400cr gives EPS Rs13.75-14.87 and sustainable ROE 13.8-14.9%, and even that ROE level was reached mainly by levering total assets/net worth from 5.24x to 7.59x, a one-time lever. Leg 1 (normalised EPS ~Rs14.5 at 9.5-12.5x, the band a AAA-rated sovereign-risk lender with compressing NIM deserves when PFC/REC-type peers earning 18-20% ROE fetch 6-9x) gives Rs133-186; Leg 2 (two-stage residual income on BVPS Rs102.6-109.8, ROE 13.5-16%, CoE 12-14%, g 9.4%) gives Rs105-160, because a ~1.5pt spread over cost of equity simply cannot justify much above 1.2-1.3x book. Intersecting them lands at Rs134-168 versus 1.78x book and ~13.5x normalised earnings today, so the current Rs195.10 embeds either a repeat of a non-repeatable tax credit or a NIM stabilisation that three years of data contradict. The bull case is not absurd - if the book compounds 20% with NIM held at 2.75-2.86%, FY27 EPS is ~Rs17.3-18.2 and the stock is only ~11x forward - which is why this is REDUCE on ~16% overvaluation rather than AVOID.

IFCI.method_1: Justified P/B off sustainable ROE — Gordon (ROE-g)/(CoE-g) with sustainable ROE 6-9%, CoE 13-14%, g 5%, applied to FY26 reported net worth of Rs 8,944.43 cr; floored at 0.35-0.75x book for asset backing (Rs 7,102 cr cash, StockHolding stake, land) and government recap/merger optionality. Gives Rs 3,131-6,708 cr equity value.
IFCI.method_2: Distributable-cash capitalisation — sustainable cash return of Rs 150-250 cr (FY26 dividends paid 148.64, FY26 FCF 220.68, against a 4-yr cumulative operating cash flow of MINUS 1,027.71 cr) capitalised at CoE 12-13% with g 5-6%. Gives Rs 1,969-4,417 cr equity value.
IFCI.methods_are_independent: Leg 1 is driven by accounting book value and accounting ROE; Leg 2 is driven by cash actually generated and returned to shareholders. For IFCI these two have diverged violently and are not linked by any identity: the effective tax rate ran 68% (FY24), 53% (FY25), 17% (FY26), so reported PAT is dominated by deferred-tax movements rather than cash earnings, and operating cash flow was negative in two of the last four years (cumulative FY23-26 OCF of MINUS 1,027.71 cr against cumulative PAT of PLUS 904.59 cr). An asset-rich but under-earning entity pushes Leg 1 well above Leg 2 (which is what happens here, Rs 4.97-10.65 vs Rs 3.13-7.01 per share); a cash-generative but thin-book entity would push Leg 2 above Leg 1. I deliberately avoided pairing justified P/B with a P/E multiple, since P/B = P/E x ROE is an arithmetic identity and would have manufactured false agreement — exactly the trap flagged.
IFCI.rationale: IFCI is a state-owned former DFI now running largely in run-off: total income has fallen three years running (1,986.59 to 1,876.09 to 1,828.71 cr), FY26 PAT of 434.71 cr on net worth of 8,944.43 cr is a 4.86% ROE (about 4.4% once the flattering 17% tax rate is normalised to 25%), and four-year cumulative operating cash flow is MINUS 1,027.71 cr — this is a business earning far below any plausible cost of equity, so it must trade at a discount to book, not a premium. Leg 1 (justified P/B, sustainable ROE 6-9%, CoE 13-14%, g 5%, floored at 0.35-0.75x book for the Rs 7,102 cr cash pile, StockHolding stake, land and government restructuring optionality) gives Rs 3,131-6,708 cr, or Rs 4.97-10.65 per share; Leg 2 (capitalising Rs 150-250 cr of distributable cash at 12-13% CoE, g 5-6%) gives Rs 1,969-4,417 cr, or Rs 3.13-7.01 per share. Intersecting, and allowing the upper end a premium for hidden and optional value that neither leg captures, I would defend Rs 5-12 per share (Rs 3,150-7,560 cr, i.e. 0.35-0.85x book and 7-17x FY26 PAT). At Rs 76.54 the stock is on 5.4x book and 111x earnings for a sub-cost-of-capital state lender — that is a speculative re-rating on consolidation/restructuring headlines, not a valuation. CAVEAT: reported share capital of Rs 2,694.31 cr at Rs 10 face value implies about 269.4 cr shares, not the 630.01 cr the API returns (FY26 financing cash flow is minus 148.64 cr, dividends only, so no issuance occurred); I used the mandated denominator so the band sits on the same ruler as the engine — on 269.4 cr shares the identical equity-value band becomes Rs 11.7-28.1 per share and the AVOID verdict is unchanged.

INDIASHLTR.method_1: Normalised forward earnings multiple. FY26 PAT 503.15 cr / 11.19 cr shares = EPS 44.96. FY27E PAT growth 25% (AUM growth decelerating from 36% to ~25%, some operating leverage left) -> EPS 56.2. Haircut 12% for normalisation: through-cycle credit cost for a 50-55% LTV self-employed affordable-housing book is ~0.6-0.9% of AUM vs the ~0.4% currently implied (4-7% of PAT), plus ~50bp of yield/spread compression from bank and PE-backed competition (~7% of PAT) -> normalised FY27E EPS ~49.5. Multiple 14x-19x, grounded in the Gordon lender identity P/E = (1 - g/ROE)/(CoE - g): at ROE 18%, g 12%, CoE 14% this yields 16.7x, so 14x-19x brackets the fundamental anchor rather than importing a peer print. Range Rs 693 - 940.
INDIASHLTR.method_2: Balance-sheet anchor: two-stage residual income / justified P/B off reported net worth. B0 = 3,198.12 cr. ROE path 17.5% -> 18% for 4 years, fading to 15-16% by year 10; retention ~89% (FY26 dividend 53.97 cr on PAT 503.15) funds ~16% book growth with no dilution; terminal g 10%. Discounting the ROE-CoE spread on opening book: at CoE 14% with terminal ROE 15% the build gives equity of ~4,840 cr (Rs 433/sh, 1.5x book); at CoE 13% with terminal ROE 16% it gives ~7,850 cr (Rs 702/sh, 2.46x book). Cross-checked against the single-stage 1 + (ROE-CoE)/(CoE-g): 2.0x at CoE 14%/g 10%, 2.8x at CoE 13.5%/g 11%. Warranted P/B 1.9x-2.6x applied to one-year-forward BVPS of ~330 (285.8 compounded at ~15.6%) -> Rs 627 - 859.
INDIASHLTR.methods_are_independent: Yes, and they materially disagreed before I reconciled them. Leg 1 is driven by the LEVEL of next year's PAT and a market-cleared earnings multiple; it barely moves with the discount rate. Leg 2 is driven almost entirely by the SPREAD of long-run sustainable ROE over cost of equity and by terminal growth, and it barely moves with next year's EPS - at CoE 14% and terminal ROE 15% it says Rs ~433 (1.5x book) while Leg 1 on the identical FY27 earnings says Rs ~820. That is a 90% divergence on the same financials, which is the opposite of the P/E-vs-EV/EBITDA arithmetic trap. They only overlap once CoE is set at 13-13.5%; the overlap is an assumption I had to defend, not an artefact. I deliberately excluded a cash-flow leg: OCF is -1,185 cr because loan disbursement is an operating outflow for a lender, so FCF yield here is not a valuation signal but a growth signal, and a replacement/asset leg is meaningless for a book of receivables (fixed assets are 27 cr on a 9,615 cr balance sheet).
INDIASHLTR.rationale: India Shelter is an affordable housing financier with a genuinely improving franchise: total income compounded 36.7% and PAT 47.9% over three years, cost-to-income fell from 43.7% to 33.3%, ROE climbed 14% -> 15.1% -> 17.0%, and leverage is only 3.0x versus 4.0-4.5x for mature HFCs, so ROE can keep rising without an equity raise. The normalised-earnings leg (14-19x on FY27E EPS of ~49.5 after a 12% haircut for through-cycle credit cost and yield compression) gives Rs 693-940; the residual-income/justified-P/B leg (1.9-2.6x on forward BVPS of ~330, driven by an 18% sustainable ROE against a 13-14% CoE and 10% terminal growth) gives Rs 627-859, and it collapses to ~Rs 433 if I use a 14% CoE with a 15% terminal ROE. Intersecting them gives Rs 693-859, which I widen to Rs 660-870 because the CoE assumption alone swings Leg 2 by 60% and this book has never been through a downturn. At 726.5 the stock trades at 2.54x book and 16.2x trailing for a 17%-ROE, 30%-growth secured lender - defensible but not cheap; it sits in the lower third of my band, so the honest call is HOLD rather than a buy, with the whole thesis hinging on whether the implied ~0.4% credit cost survives the first real cycle.

INOXWIND.method_1: Normalised-earnings multiple: FY26 PAT Rs 449 cr (EPS Rs 2.65) haircut to mid-cycle margin but credited for the volume ramp gives normalised PAT of Rs 430-520 cr; applying 19-24x (cyclical wind-turbine OEM with a secular India demand tailwind but sub-cost-of-capital returns and a 2-year execution record, so no franchise multiple; global WTG peers earn only 4-8% EBITDA) implies Rs 48-74 per share.
INOXWIND.method_2: Balance-sheet anchor via justified P/B = (ROE - g)/(CoE - g): book value Rs 6,382 cr = Rs 37.66/share; sustainable ROE 10-16% (FY26 actual 8.3% on average equity, allowing for partial working-capital normalisation and operating leverage), CoE 12.5%, g 5.5% gives 0.64-1.50x book = Rs 24-57 per share. Cross-checked against cash: cumulative FY23-26 FCF of -Rs 4,116 cr and 353-day receivables mean no cash-flow leg supports a higher anchor.
INOXWIND.methods_are_independent: Yes, and here they diverge sharply. Leg 1 accepts the reported income statement and asks what multiple the profit stream deserves; Leg 2 ignores the P&L entirely and asks what a rupee of the company's equity capital is worth given the return that capital actually earns. The mechanical link between the two is broken by this balance sheet: PAT of Rs 449 cr sits on Rs 6,382 cr of equity and Rs 12,067 cr of assets, so a superficially ordinary 29x P/E coexists with an 8.3% ROE and 6.5% ROIC. The legs are not a restatement of each other - one produced Rs 74 at its top and the other Rs 24 at its bottom, a 3x spread, which is only possible because asset intensity (receivables at 97% of revenue) is doing independent work in Leg 2 that Leg 1 cannot see. I deliberately avoided P/E vs EV/EBITDA, which for FY26 (EBITDA 891, PAT 449, interest 200, D&A 204, tax 32%) would have been the same arithmetic twice.
INOXWIND.rationale: Leg 1 (normalised earnings): FY26 revenue Rs 4,397 cr, EBITDA Rs 891 cr (20.3%), PAT Rs 449 cr; normalised PAT of Rs 430-520 cr at a cyclical-OEM 19-24x gives Rs 48-74. Leg 2 (justified P/B): book Rs 37.66/share, sustainable ROE 10-16% vs CoE 12.5% and g 5.5% gives 0.64-1.50x = Rs 24-57. The tiebreaker is cash quality: receivables are Rs 4,250 cr against Rs 4,397 cr of revenue (353 days, up from 72% of sales in FY25), FY26 OCF was -Rs 598 cr despite PAT of Rs 449 cr, cumulative FY23-26 FCF is -Rs 4,116 cr funded by two equity raises, and ROIC is only 6.5% - so reported profit is not yet cash and the earnings leg's own low end is generous. I would defend Rs 40-60 (centre Rs 50 = 1.3x book, ~10x EV/EBITDA, 19x FY26 EPS), which is a real credit to a genuine turnaround (revenue 733 to 4,397 in three years, net debt down to Rs 833 cr) without paying for forecasts. At Rs 78.14 the market implies roughly 20% sustainable ROE - a level this company has never delivered - so the price is ~30% above my band.

IREDA.method_1: Balance-sheet anchor — justified P/B = (ROE - g)/(CoE - g) on FY26 book of Rs 13,785 cr (BVPS 49.51), cross-checked with a 10-year FCFE-to-equity model. Sustainable ROE 14-17% (FY24/25/26 = 17.3/18.0/15.6%, trending DOWN as equity raises dilute and credit costs bite); CoE 13.5-15.0% (Rf ~6.75% + ERP 6% x beta 1.2-1.4 for a concentrated, high-beta PSU mid-cap); terminal g 8-10%. Gives P/B 1.0x-1.6x on trailing book, 1.15x-1.72x rolled to a mid-FY27 book of ~Rs 52-54. The FCFE build (PAT at ROA 2.10-2.25% less the equity needed to hold ~14% equity/assets while assets grow 18% tapering to 9%) independently lands at Rs 51 (CoE 14.5%, g 8.5%) to Rs 85 (CoE 13.5%, g 9%) — note FCFE is NEGATIVE for the first two years, because the business consumes external equity to grow. LEG 1 RANGE: Rs 52-85.
IREDA.method_2: Market-relative normalised earnings multiple against listed Indian lender comps — uses observed peer prices only, no CoE or terminal-growth input. Normalised EPS: FY26 credit cost of Rs 904 cr (derived: NII 3,374.52 - SGA 105.55 - dep 43.89 - EBIT 2,321.30) is 1.04% of avg assets vs 0.31% in FY25 and a write-back in FY24; normalising to 0.80-0.85% through-cycle for concentrated renewable project finance gives PAT ~Rs 2,007 cr, EPS ~7.20, and a one-year-forward EPS of ~7.7-8.0. Peer P/E pulled live: PFC 5.4x (ROE 26.8%), RECLTD 6.1x (20.0%), HUDCO 9.7x (20.2%), CANFINHOME 10.1x (19.7%), LICHSGFIN 5.1x (14.4%), IRFC 16.6x (12.8%, excluded as a sovereign-pass-through/float anomaly). Median ex-IRFC ~7.5x. IREDA earns a growth premium (book compounding 18-22% vs peers' 10-14%, structural RE runway, Navratna status) but a discount for a LOWER ROE than PFC/REC/HUDCO/CANFIN and tripling credit costs — net 8x-12x on EPS 7.0-8.0. LEG 2 RANGE: Rs 56-96.
IREDA.methods_are_independent: Partially, and I will state the limit honestly rather than overclaim. For any lender P/B = P/E x ROE, so the two legs are not orthogonal in the way an earnings multiple and a cash-flow yield are for an industrial. They are nonetheless set by disjoint evidence and can genuinely diverge on three axes. (1) Different discount evidence: Leg 1 is a closed-form intrinsic construct using only IREDA's own ROE plus MY assumed CoE and terminal g, and knows nothing about what anyone pays for lenders today; Leg 2 uses six observed peer market prices and uses no CoE or g input at all. They separate exactly when the market's implied CoE differs from my 13.5-15% — which is the whole question for a stock at 2.4x book. (2) Opposite treatment of the credit-cycle: Leg 2 ADDS BACK excess FY26 provisions to get normalised earnings power, while Leg 1 works off reported book that has already ABSORBED them; these push in opposite directions. (3) They did in fact disagree at the top: Leg 1 caps at Rs 85 because the ROE-CoE spread is thin (~1-2pp), whereas Leg 2 reaches Rs 96 because HUDCO/CANFIN show the market paying ~10x earnings for PSU lenders — but those peers earn 20% ROE, so I took the lower ceiling. The overlap is 56-85, not an identity. The Gordon leg is also structurally unstable here precisely because ROE approximately equals CoE, which is the substantive finding, not an artefact.
IREDA.rationale: IREDA is a Navratna PSU NBFC-IFC lending to Indian renewable projects: real growth (assets 50,447 to 93,808 cr over four years, revenue 3,470 to 8,279 cr) but a thinning return profile — ROE fell from 18.0% (FY25) to 15.6% (FY26) as equity raises diluted and derived credit costs tripled from Rs 271 cr to Rs 904 cr (1.04% of avg assets), leaving PAT growth at just +10.3% versus +35.6% the prior year. Leg 1 (justified P/B 1.0-1.6x on BVPS 49.51, ROE 14-17% vs CoE 13.5-15%, g 8-10%; FCFE cross-check Rs 51-85) gives Rs 52-85; Leg 2 (8-12x normalised EPS of 7.0-8.0, against PFC 5.4x/REC 6.1x/HUDCO 9.7x/CANFIN 10.1x) gives Rs 56-96; the intersection is Rs 56-85, midpoint ~70. The central judgement is that IREDA earns roughly its own cost of equity, so growing the book fast creates little value per rupee — it consumes external capital (FCFE negative for two years) — yet the stock is priced at 2.42x book and 17.8x earnings while PFC earns 26.8% ROE at 1.37x book and REC 20.0% at 1.16x. My Rs 85 ceiling is already a heroic 1.72x book for a 15.6%-ROE lender, and the price sits 41% above it. The main risk to my band being too low is the scarcity/float premium (GoI ~75%, only listed pure-play RE financier) and a re-rate if ROE recovers to 18-20% while CoE compresses — but that is market microstructure and hope, not demonstrated intrinsic economics, and the FY26 credit-cost print argues the other way.

JKTYRE.method_1: Normalised-earnings multiple. Through-cycle EBITDA margin of 11.1% (FY23-26: 8.5/13.8/10.7/11.6%) applied to a ~Rs 17,000 cr revenue base gives normalised EBITDA ~Rs 1,900 cr; less D&A ~550 (stepping up as the ramp capitalises) and interest ~370, taxed at 26%, gives normalised PAT of Rs 670-780 cr (EPS Rs 24-30). Multiple of 10-14x: a leveraged (2.4x net debt/EBITDA), sub-WACC-ROIC (9.9% post-tax) commodity-input tyre maker gets a cyclical multiple, not the franchise multiple of an MRF or a Balkrishna, but TBR replacement leadership and a deleveraging trend justify the upper half in a good year. Range: 670x10 = Rs 236/sh to 780x14 = Rs 384/sh, centre 720x12 = Rs 304/sh.
JKTYRE.method_2: Sustainable free-cash-flow capitalisation. Reported FCF was 761 / 840 / 78 / 20 cr across FY23-26 — four-year average Rs 425 cr — because capex (avg 825, FY26 1,424) ran at 1.86x depreciation. Two anchors: (a) zero-growth steady state, EBITDA 1,900 less cash interest 377, cash tax ~300 and true maintenance capex ~600 = FCFE Rs 623 cr, capitalised at a 9-10% required yield for a leveraged cyclical = Rs 219-244/sh; (b) post-ramp, crediting the new capacity — FCFE of Rs 750-900 cr by FY29 capitalised at 11.5-12% less 3.5-4% growth and discounted back three years = Rs 221-305/sh. Range Rs 220-305, centre ~Rs 260.
JKTYRE.methods_are_independent: They diverge precisely because JK Tyre is mid-capex-ramp. Leg 1 charges operations only book depreciation (~Rs 500-550 cr); Leg 2 charges the Rs 900-950 cr of actual cash capex the business needs to hold and grow share at a gross-block asset turn of only 1.19x, plus a 23%-of-sales working-capital block that absorbs ~Rs 230 cr per Rs 1,000 cr of revenue growth. Over FY23-26 the company spent Rs 3,300 cr of capex against Rs 1,772 cr of D&A, so the wedge is large and real, not a modelling artefact. The direct evidence they disagree: between FY25 and FY26 PAT rose from 516 to 774 cr while free cash fell from 78 to 20 cr — earnings and cash moved in opposite directions. They would only collapse into one method if capex equalled depreciation, which has not happened in any of the four years. I deliberately did NOT use EV/EBITDA as the second leg since it is mechanically the same statement as the P/E leg; I used it only as an internal consistency check on Leg 1.
JKTYRE.rationale: JK Tyre is a leveraged, capital-hungry cyclical, not a franchise: FY26 revenue Rs 16,327 cr, EBITDA Rs 1,890 cr (11.6%, against a four-year average of 11.1% and a range of 8.5-13.8%), PAT Rs 774 cr, net worth Rs 6,061 cr, net debt Rs 4,587 cr (2.4x EBITDA, interest cover 3.8x), post-tax ROIC 9.9% and four-year average ROE of ~13.5%. The normalised-earnings leg gives Rs 236-384 (centre Rs 304); the sustainable-cash-flow leg gives Rs 220-305 (centre Rs 260), the gap being the Rs 350-400 cr of annual capex above depreciation that earnings ignore and cash flow does not. An independent justified-P/B cross-check — (ROE 13-15% less g 5%) over (CoE 12-12.5% less g 5%) on book of Rs 6,061 cr — lands at Rs 227-305, corroborating the lower-to-middle part of the intersection. I intersect at Rs 235-305, which at the top implies 12x normalised earnings, 7.0x normalised EBITDA and 1.43x book — a full price for a business earning below its cost of capital. At Rs 399.75 the market is capitalising a good year (it needs ~Rs 950 cr of PAT on a 12.5% margin, achieved only once in four years) at 14.7x trailing, 19x four-year-average earnings and 1.87x book, leaving the price 31% above my upper bound.

JTEKTINDIA.method_1: Normalised mid-cycle earnings multiple: FY29 revenue 3,350-3,650 cr at 8.5-10.0% EBITDA margin, less D&A ~150 cr, interest ~25 cr, 26% tax -> normalised PAT 91-158 cr, capitalised at 15-18x and discounted ~3 years at 12.5% CoE.
JTEKTINDIA.method_2: Owner cash-flow / FCF-yield anchor: mature-state FCFF of 95-140 cr (EBITDA less cash tax on EBIT, less maintenance capex set equal to D&A ~140-150 cr, less working-capital growth), valued at a required 7-9% FCF yield (11-14x FCFF), less net debt of 267 cr.
JTEKTINDIA.methods_are_independent: Leg A capitalises accrual profit and is driven by the margin-recovery assumption and the P/E chosen; Leg B ignores accounting profit entirely and is driven by the capital-consumption ratio (maintenance capex vs D&A) and working-capital intensity. They diverge exactly when reported earnings and cash generation part company, which is this company's actual record: PAT of 87/107/75/77 cr over FY23-26 against FCF of -2/-23/-85/-345 cr (cumulative -455 cr), funded by borrowings rising 62 -> 340 cr plus a ~325 cr equity raise. A name with light capex and negative working capital would score far better on Leg B than Leg A; JTEKT scores worse, and the gap between Rs 35-72 and Rs 28-61 is precisely the unresolved question of whether the doubled asset base ever stops eating the earnings. This is deliberately NOT a P/E-vs-EV/EBITDA pair, which would be one method restated (here D&A is 45%+ of EBITDA, so a "normal" 10x EV/EBITDA silently equals ~23x P/E).
JTEKTINDIA.rationale: JTEKT India is a capital-intensive Tier-1 steering-systems supplier with heavy Maruti concentration, mid-way through doubling its asset base: net fixed assets 477 -> 1,211 cr and capex 97 -> 195 -> 279 -> 444 cr since FY23, yet EBITDA margin fell 9.9% -> 7.7% -> 7.3% and absolute EBIT actually declined from 141.4 cr (FY24) to 95.1 cr (FY26) despite revenue up 19%; ROCE fell 16.4% -> 6.6% and FCF was negative in all four years (cumulative -455 cr), funded by borrowings 62 -> 340 cr plus a ~325 cr equity issue. Leg A (normalised earnings) puts FY29 PAT at 91-158 cr on revenue of 3,350-3,650 cr at an 8.5-10.0% EBITDA margin; at 15-18x discounted three years that is Rs 35-72/share. Leg B (owner cash flow) gives mature FCFF of 95-140 cr after cash tax, maintenance capex of ~140-150 cr and working-capital growth; at an 11-14x FCFF multiple less 267 cr net debt that is Rs 28-61/share. Intersecting and leaning to the upper half of the overlap to credit capacity that is commissioned but not yet loaded gives Rs 42-75 (centre ~Rs 58), equivalent to 1.0-1.7x the Rs 43/share book and 15-27x FY26 PAT of 76.9 cr. At Rs 140.71 the market pays ~3.3x book, ~21x EV/EBITDA and ~49x trailing PAT for a business currently earning ~7% ROE on a shrinking-return capital base, which embeds an EPS/EV content re-rating and parent-delisting optionality I cannot underwrite from the financials.

KIRLOSBROS.method_1: Normalised earnings multiple: mid-cycle EBITDA margin 12.2% on Rs 4,538 cr revenue = Rs 553 cr, less D&A 100, plus ~84 cr recurring interest income on the Rs 1,200 cr cash/investment pile, less 45 cr interest, tax normalised to 26% (FY26 reported only 20.1%) -> normalised PAT ~Rs 364 cr, EPS ~Rs 47.5 on 7.68 cr shares. Multiple 20-28x: premium to market for a market-leading pump brand with ~20% core ROE and net cash, but capped below franchise levels because EBITDA margin is only 11-13%, revenue is project-linked and just went flat, and the Kirloskar family governance history warrants a discount. Range Rs 950-1,330, centre ~1,140.
KIRLOSBROS.method_2: Normalised free-cash-flow yield: normalised OCF = PAT 364 + D&A 100 = 464, less ~82 cr structural working-capital absorption (20% NWC/sales intensity on ~9% revenue growth) = ~382 cr, which brackets actual OCF of 334-386; less normalised capex Rs 125 cr (4-yr actual 90-135, D&A 100) -> normalised FCF ~Rs 257 cr, range 220-270. Required FCF yield 2.8-4.0% (25-36x FCF) for a net-cash quality Indian industrial growing high-single-digit. Range Rs 716-1,255, centre ~985. Reported FCF has been 196/246/296/199 cr, 4-yr average 234, so the normalisation is not generous.
KIRLOSBROS.methods_are_independent: They move on different drivers and in fact disagree (earnings centre ~1,140 vs cash centre ~985). KBL's PAT and its free cash flow have decoupled: FY26 PAT was Rs 361 cr but FCF only Rs 199 cr, because working capital absorbed Rs 258 cr on flat revenue (NWC/sales 18.2%->23.7%, receivable days 41->63, inventory 918->1,072). Cash conversion is ~55-70% and deteriorating, so the earnings leg is set by EBITDA margin and the tax rate (which swung 27.8%->20.1% in one year), while the cash leg is set by working-capital intensity and capex - neither of which appears in the P/E. This is deliberately NOT a P/E-vs-EV/EBITDA pair, which would be one method restated. A third, non-scoring cross-check (justified P/B = (ROE-g)/(CoE-g) with 20% core ROE ex-cash, CoE 11.5-12.5%, g 8% -> 2.2-3.4x operating equity plus Rs 951 cr cash/investments = Rs 650-800) sits below both legs, confirming the divergence is real and pulling weight toward the low end rather than the high.
KIRLOSBROS.rationale: Leg 1 (normalised earnings, EPS ~Rs 47.5 at 20-28x) gives Rs 950-1,330; Leg 2 (normalised FCF ~Rs 257 cr at a required 2.8-4.0% yield) gives Rs 716-1,255; a justified-P/B cross-check gives Rs 650-800. Key figures: market cap Rs 14,362 cr (1870.1 x 7.68 cr shares), net cash Rs 633 cr plus Rs 318 cr investments, FY26 revenue Rs 4,538 cr (+1.0%), EBITDA Rs 506 cr (-16%, margin 13.4%->11.1%), PAT Rs 361 cr flattered by a 20.1% tax rate, OCF Rs 334 cr, FCF Rs 199 cr, ROE 15.9% (from 21.2%). This is a genuinely good business - India's largest pump maker, ~20% ROE on operating capital, net cash, real export optionality - but FY26 shows the earnings engine stalling while working capital consumes a rising share of profit, and none of that supports a 39.8x trailing P/E, 27.2x EV/EBITDA and 1.4% FCF yield. I defend Rs 900-1,250 (19-26x normalised earnings, 11-16x EV/EBITDA, 2.8-3.7% FCF yield); the current price sits ~50% above the top, which requires FY28 EBITDA margins back at 14% on Rs 5,500 cr revenue simply to justify today's quote. Verdict AVOID on price, not on business quality.

KIRLOSENG.method_1: Consolidated earnings multiple. FY26 PAT 557.72 cr / 14.24 cr shares = EPS Rs 39.17. Applied 28-38x, where the multiple is itself a profit-weighted blend: ~33x on the ~85% of profit from the engines/gensets/pumps franchise (15.3% revenue CAGR FY23-26, 5,024 to 7,701 cr; asset-light at ~6x turns on 1,077 cr net fixed assets; genuine brand and CPCB-IV+ pricing tailwind, but cyclical with only ~12% product margins, so not a 45x consumer-franchise multiple) and ~12x on the ~15% of profit from Arka Fincap, a sub-scale lender. Range: Rs 1,097-1,488.
KIRLOSENG.method_2: Sum-of-the-parts: enterprise cash earnings for the manufacturer plus a pure balance-sheet anchor for the lender. Carved manufacturing EBITDA out of consolidated EBITDA (1,379.87 cr less ~575 cr of NBFC pre-interest earnings, i.e. Arka PBT ~135 cr grossed back up by its ~442 cr interest cost) = ~803 cr, an 11.8% margin on ~6,800 cr of product revenue - which independently reconciles with KOEL's known standalone margin profile. Valued at 17-23x EV/EBITDA (band 750-870 cr on carve-out error) against roughly nil manufacturing net debt, since all 4,285 cr of consolidated net debt sits at the NBFC. Added Arka at 0.7-1.2x its ~1,400 cr equity - below book on a strict basis because it earns only ~7-8% ROE against a ~14% cost of equity, up to ~1.2x on strategic-sale optionality. Range: Rs 938-1,499.
KIRLOSENG.methods_are_independent: They share no valuation primitive. Leg 1 multiplies the consolidated bottom line; Leg 2 never touches PAT at all - it prices pre-interest, pre-tax, pre-D&A manufacturing cash earnings at an enterprise multiple and prices the lender purely off its equity base. The usual "PAT is a fixed function of EBITDA" objection specifically fails here for two structural reasons. First, the entire Rs 442 cr interest line and the Rs 4,285 cr of net debt belong to Arka Fincap, so the bridge from consolidated EBITDA down to consolidated PAT runs straight through a segment that Leg 2 refuses to apply an earnings multiple to at all - Leg 1 implicitly pays a blended franchise multiple on NBFC profit, Leg 2 explicitly pays only book for it. Second, the company is mid-capex-ramp: D&A is up 66% in three years (104.7 to 174.1 cr) on capex running ~2x depreciation, so EBITDA and PAT are actively diverging rather than tracking. They can and do disagree in the obvious direction: Arka is ~39% of consolidated equity but only ~15% of profit, so the book-anchored leg prints materially below the blended P/E; conversely, if the true manufacturing margin were 9% rather than 12%, Leg 2 collapses ~25% while Leg 1 is almost unmoved. That both legs happened to centre near Rs 1,200 is a result, not an identity.
KIRLOSENG.rationale: KIRLOSENG consolidated is a hybrid: a high-quality diesel engine/genset/pump franchise compounding revenue at 15.3% (5,024 to 7,701 cr FY23-FY26) bolted to Arka Fincap, an NBFC that accounts for essentially all of the Rs 5,374 cr borrowings, the Rs 442 cr interest expense, and the deeply negative operating cash flow of FY23-FY25 (-920, -469, -739 cr) that flipped to +932 cr only when the loan book stopped growing - so consolidated EBITDA margin of 17.9% overstates a genuine manufacturing margin of roughly 12%, and any EV/EBITDA read on the headline figure is simply wrong. Leg 1 (28-38x FY26 EPS of Rs 39.17, blended down for the NBFC's profit share) gives Rs 1,097-1,488; Leg 2 (manufacturing EBITDA ~803 cr at 17-23x, nil manufacturing net debt, plus Arka at 0.7-1.2x its ~1,400 cr book) gives Rs 938-1,499. I would defend Rs 1,100-1,500 to a PM, midpoint ~Rs 1,300, with the width reflecting real uncertainty in the segment carve-out rather than in the direction of the answer. At Rs 2,189.8 the stock is 55.9x trailing earnings and 8.6x consolidated book on a 16.6% ROE; backing out even a generous Rs 1,400 cr for Arka leaves the manufacturing arm on ~37x EV/EBITDA, a cycle-peak narrative multiple for a 12%-margin cyclical, not an intrinsic value. A Gordon cross-check reinforces this - even crediting the manufacturing arm its standalone ~21% ROE, justified P/B lands nowhere near 8.6x - though I deliberately did not use it as a leg given its instability when g approaches CoE.

LMW.method_1: Normalised through-cycle earnings multiple: mid-cycle revenue Rs 4,100 cr at 8% EBITDA margin (vs 9.6% FY23 peak / 4.7% FY25 trough) less D&A Rs 120 cr, taxed 25% = operating NOPAT ~Rs 155 cr; plus after-tax treasury income ~Rs 115 cr on the Rs 2,246 cr cash+investments pile = mid-cycle PAT ~Rs 270 cr (vs FY23-26 actuals of 384/374/103/131). Applied 16-24x: low end is the DCF-justified 11-13x for ~5% growth at 18% mid-cycle ROIC and 12% CoE, high end credits the dominant domestic spinning-machinery franchise and upcycle optionality. Gives Rs 4,320-6,480 cr equity = Rs 4,040-6,060/share.
LMW.method_2: Realised cash generation plus discounted treasury: FY23-26 average OCF Rs 178 cr less maintenance capex ~Rs 110 cr (approx D&A run-rate Rs 102 cr) = Rs 68 cr; mid-cycle normalised operating FCF ~Rs 145 cr. Capitalised Rs 80-150 cr at 12-16x (12% CoE, ~4-5% terminal growth) = operating value Rs 960-2,400 cr. Added treasury of Rs 1,602 cr cash + Rs 644 cr investments at a 10-25% discount (idle for years, earning ~7% pre-tax against ~12% CoE; dividend actually cut from Rs 105 cr FY24 to Rs 32 cr FY26) = Rs 1,690-2,020 cr. Gives Rs 2,650-4,420 cr equity = Rs 2,480-4,130/share. Balance-sheet cross-check: justified P/B = (ROE-g)/(CoE-g) = 0.7x at 9.4% mid-cycle ROE, 1.8x even at 16.4% peak ROE, versus 6.0x paid.
LMW.methods_are_independent: Leg 1 is an accrual earnings multiple built from assumed mid-cycle revenue and margin; Leg 2 is built from realised cash actually collected across the cycle plus a balance-sheet treasury value. They are not one method restated, because for LMW accrual profit and operating cash have diverged materially: cumulative FY23-26 PAT was Rs 991 cr while cumulative operating FCF was only Rs 78 cr (OCF Rs 711 cr less capex Rs 633 cr). Two structural wedges drive that gap and either could resolve in favour of one leg over the other. First, a large and growing share of reported PAT is treasury/other income (FY26 PBT Rs 182 cr against EBIT of just Rs 37 cr) which is booked outside operating cash flow, so the earnings leg can look healthy while the operating business generates almost nothing. Second, capex has run at 1.3-2.3x depreciation with gross block up only Rs 297 cr against Rs 633 cr spent, so if that spend is genuine growth capex the cash leg is too harsh and the legs converge upward, whereas if it is a permanent capital-intensity drag the cash leg is right and the earnings leg is an illusion. Critically, I deliberately avoided pairing P/E with EV/EBITDA off the same year, which would be arithmetic rather than corroboration. In the event the two legs did materially disagree (Leg 1 centre ~Rs 5,050/sh vs Leg 2 centre ~Rs 3,300/sh, a 53% spread), which is exactly the honest disagreement the pairing was chosen to surface, and my band spans both rather than pretending to a narrow intersection.
LMW.rationale: LMW is India's dominant textile spinning-machinery maker but the financials show a flat-to-shrinking, thin-margin cyclical, not a compounder: revenue Rs 4,719 cr (FY23) to Rs 3,207 cr (FY26), EBITDA margin halved from 9.6% to 4.9%, PAT down from Rs 384 cr to Rs 131 cr, and net working capital dead flat at ~Rs 400 cr so the weak cash is structural rather than a reversible build. Leg 1 (mid-cycle PAT ~Rs 270 cr at 16-24x) gives Rs 4,040-6,060/share; Leg 2 (through-cycle operating FCF Rs 80-150 cr at 12-16x plus Rs 2,246 cr treasury at a 10-25% discount) gives Rs 2,480-4,130/share. I defend Rs 3,500-6,200 with a centre near Rs 4,850, which still pays roughly 19x mid-cycle NOPAT for the operating business after netting the cash, generous for a franchise whose net operating capital is only Rs 860 cr and whose revenue has gone nowhere in four years. At Rs 16,152 the market cap of Rs 17,283 cr is 132x FY26 EPS, 45x peak FY23 EPS, 6.0x book and 5.4x sales, which requires revenue to nearly double AND EBITDA margin to reach 12% (above its own historical peak) AND a 30x multiple to persist. That is an expectation the last four years of statements contradict, so AVOID; the main risk to my view is a genuine structural upcycle in Indian spinning capex plus the aerospace/machine-tools diversification scaling far faster than any historical margin evidence supports.

LUMAXIND.method_1: Normalised earnings multiple: 16-22x normalised PAT of Rs 155-172 cr (FY26 EBITDA margin haircut 9.3%->9.0%, D&A stepped to ~160, modest interest true-up), cross-checked against justified P/B = (ROE-g)/(CoE-g) -> Rs 2,700-4,000
LUMAXIND.method_2: Owner-earnings / FCFF: OCF less normalised maintenance capex (~1.15x D&A = Rs 175 cr) capitalised, plus a 5-year FCFF DCF charging the ramp capex and working capital (terminal g 5.5-6%, WACC 11-11.5%, terminal incremental ROIC 12-18%) -> Rs 1,500-2,900
LUMAXIND.methods_are_independent: They read opposite sides of the capex ramp and have literally disagreed in sign. The P&L leg sees capex capitalised onto the balance sheet and released slowly as D&A (3.6% of sales), so PAT rose 67% from Rs 103 cr to Rs 172.5 cr over FY23-26. The cash leg charges the capex as it is spent (7-8% of sales, Rs 289-324 cr/yr), so cumulative FCF over the same four years was MINUS Rs 142 cr. One says the business earns Rs 172 cr a year; the other says it has produced no free cash in four years. The legs are reconciled only by an assumption neither contains - whether capex is a finite capacity build (Rs 3,000+/sh) or a permanent 7%-of-sales run rate (Rs 1,400-1,800/sh) - which is why they span 50%+ rather than agreeing arithmetically. This is not P/E vs EV/EBITDA restated: the driver of the gap (capital intensity and its reversibility) is absent from the earnings leg entirely.
LUMAXIND.rationale: Lumax Industries is India's #1 auto-lighting Tier-1 (Stanley Electric technology tie-up) compounding revenue at 21.7% (Rs 2,320 cr FY23 -> Rs 4,184 cr FY26), but the growth has not been value-creative: EBIT margin is flat at 5.5%->5.6% despite 80% more revenue, ROIC is ~10-11%, and incremental ROIC is 10.9% (delta-NOPAT Rs 84 cr on delta-invested-capital Rs 772 cr) - at or below a ~11.5% WACC, so growth is roughly value-neutral and no franchise multiple is warranted. The earnings leg at 16-22x normalised PAT of Rs 155-172 cr gives Rs 2,700-4,000 (justified P/B of 2.2-4.0x on 19-22% ROE independently corroborates Rs 2,200-3,900); the cash leg, charging Rs 175 cr maintenance capex against Rs 377 cr normalised EBITDA and Rs 55 cr cash tax, gives Rs 1,500-2,900, with no-growth capitalisation as low as Rs 440. Probability-weighting bear/base/bull (capex stuck at 7% of sales vs normalising to 5.5% vs utilisation catch-up on the already-built asset base at 11% EBITDA margins, fixed-asset turns having slipped 3.00->2.75) lands at ~Rs 3,130. I would defend Rs 2,600-3,900, widened at the top to allow that part of the Rs 973 cr borrowings is trade acceptances rather than true debt. At Rs 5,284.5 (28.5x trailing PAT, 14.9x EV/EBITDA on a 9.3%-margin, 2.2x-levered, negative-cumulative-FCF supplier) the price is ~35% above my high end and prices the bull scenario in full.

LUMAXTECH.method_1: Normalised-earnings multiple: tax-normalise FY26 PBT 405.9 cr at a 22-25% rate (vs the reported 16.9%, well below the 25.4% FY23-25 average) for ~Rs 315-330 cr of earnings power, capitalised at 20-27x -> Rs 800-1,080/sh.
LUMAXTECH.method_2: Owner cash-flow leg: two-stage FCFF DCF off NOPAT 349 cr (EBIT 464.9 at 25% tax) with ROIC 20-25%, WACC 11-11.75%, terminal growth 5-7%, plus Rs 640-700 cr for equity-accounted JVs and less Rs 842 cr net debt (Rs 490-905); cross-checked with a 3.0-4.5% FCF yield on Rs 213-250 cr sustainable FCF (Rs 575-870) -> Rs 580-900/sh.
LUMAXTECH.methods_are_independent: They can and do disagree because they are driven by different line items and different assumptions. The earnings leg reads only the P&L: PBT, a normalised tax rate, and the multiple the franchise deserves. It is blind to capital intensity. The cash leg is driven by the cash statement and balance sheet: capex 248 vs D&A 179 (1.38x), working-capital absorption, the Rs 474 cr of goodwill plus acquired intangibles that depress ROIC to 19.8% (vs 27% ex-goodwill), and Rs 842 cr of net debt. Lumax converts only 63% of reported PAT into FCF (213 vs 337) and its observed reinvestment rate of ~29% at 19.8% ROIC supports just ~6% organic growth — the rest of the 38% three-year revenue CAGR was bought via the IAC India acquisition, which never appears in the capex line the earnings multiple ignores. The result is a genuine spread: Leg 1 lands Rs 800-1,080, Leg 2 lands Rs 580-900, overlapping only in a narrow window. Deliberately excluded: EV/EBITDA (12-16x -> Rs 836-1,148) was used ONLY as a reasonableness check on Leg 1, not as a second leg, because it is mechanically the same information as the P/E once interest, D&A and tax are fixed.
LUMAXTECH.rationale: Lumax Auto Technologies is a levered, acquisitive Tier-1 auto ancillary whose technology is largely licensed through Japanese/Israeli JVs: FY23-26 revenue compounded 1,847 -> 4,870 cr and EBITDA 194 -> 644 cr (margin 10.5% -> 13.2%), but the step-up is dominated by the IAC India deal (goodwill 177 + intangibles 297) and FY26 PAT of 337 cr is flattered by a 16.9% tax rate against a 25.4% three-year average. Leg 1 (normalised earnings): ~Rs 315-330 cr of earnings power at 20-27x, the range a ~17-20% post-tax-ROIC ancillary with customer concentration, 1.0x D/E and full auto-cycle exposure earns, gives Rs 800-1,080/sh. Leg 2 (cash): OCF 460 less capex 248 = FCF 213 cr at 63% conversion; the FCFF DCF (NOPAT 349, ROIC 20-25%, WACC 11-11.75%, tg 5-7%, plus JVs, less net debt 842) gives Rs 490-905 and a 3.0-4.5% FCF yield gives Rs 575-870, so Rs 580-900/sh. I defend Rs 750-1,100 (centre ~925), the overlap nudged up for the fact that the capex is genuinely growth capex with revenue following it — that is 22-27x normalised earnings and ~13-16x EV/EBITDA. At Rs 1,568 the stock trades 43% above the top of the band on 38x trailing and 21.4x EV/EBITDA, and even a bullish FY29 path (Rs 8,000 cr revenue, ~600 cr PAT, 25x exit) discounts back to only ~Rs 1,280, so AVOID. CAVEAT: I used shares_cr = 8.24 as instructed, but FY23-26 equity capital is constant at Rs 13.63 cr, implying ~6.82 cr shares at Rs 2 face value — the 8.24 figure is plausibly a proxy that nets out minority interest; on a 6.82 cr basis the same equity values become Rs 907-1,330 and the verdict stays REDUCE/AVOID, so the call is robust even though the per-share levels are not.

M&MFIN.method_1: Normalised-earnings multiple (market-comparison leg, no cost-of-capital input). Through-cycle ROA of 1.75-1.90% applied to FY26 total assets of Rs 158,644 cr gives normalised PAT of Rs 2,780-3,015 cr, or EPS Rs 18.5-21.0 on 137.03 cr shares (FY26 reported EPS 20.88, so FY26 sits at the upper end of normal, not a blowout). Capitalised at 13-18x: a deliberate discount to 20%-ROE NBFCs (Chola, Bajaj Finance at 22-30x) because M&MFIN earns roughly 12% ROE with genuine rural/vehicle credit cyclicality, but at/above Shriram Finance's ~13-15x to credit 18% top-line CAGR, the #1-2 rural vehicle-finance franchise and M&M group parentage. Range Rs 240-378, central ~Rs 310 at 15.5x on Rs 20 EPS.
M&MFIN.method_2: Justified P/B from an absolute required-return model (no market multiple used). Sustainable ROE 12.0-13.5%: FY26 delivered 11.9% on average equity (2,861 / 24,084), the four-year record is 10.1-11.9%, and the upper end assumes the ROA improvement to ~1.9% holds while leverage rebuilds from the post-raise 6.0x back toward 6.5x. CoE 12.0-13.5% (Rf ~6.5%, ERP ~5.5-6.0%, beta ~1.1-1.2 for a cyclical NBFC); g 7.0-8.0%, consistent with 12.5% ROE x 68% retention (dividends 903 / PAT 2,861). (ROE-g)/(CoE-g) yields 1.0-1.5x, centred near 1.15x — the spread of ROE over CoE is close to zero, so growth is roughly value-neutral and the model tethers to ~1x. Applied to FY26 book of Rs 194.4/sh, haircut ~3% to Rs 188 for residual rural NPA (the nbfc block returned null GNPA/NNPA, so this is a judgemental trim, not a measured one). Range Rs 188-282, central ~Rs 230.
M&MFIN.methods_are_independent: They can genuinely diverge because they draw on different information and answer different questions. Leg 1 is relative: it takes a normalised earnings stream and asks what the market pays for comparable Indian NBFCs — it never touches cost of capital, book value, dividend policy or the FY26 equity raise. Leg 2 is absolute: it asks what a rupee of equity is worth given the spread of sustainable ROE over an independently estimated CoE — it never references a peer multiple or a traded price. The wedge between them is precisely sector re-rating: if Indian NBFCs are collectively priced above what required returns justify, Leg 1 stays permissive while Leg 2 turns austere, which is exactly what happened here (Leg 1 midpoint Rs 310 vs Leg 2 midpoint Rs 230, a 35% gap, with only Rs 240-282 of true overlap). They are not the P/E-vs-EV/EBITDA trap: I deliberately avoided a second earnings-multiple leg, and I avoided an FCF leg entirely because for a lender operating cash flow (Rs -12,772 cr in FY26) is loan-book growth, not economic burn, so an FCF yield would be meaningless rather than independent. The residual linkage — both legs are ultimately functions of earnings on equity — is unavoidable for any lender; no fundamental method for an NBFC escapes ROE, book and CoE.
M&MFIN.rationale: Leg 1 (normalised EPS Rs 18.5-21.0 at 13-18x) gives Rs 240-378; Leg 2 (justified P/B 1.0-1.5x on adjusted book of Rs 188, from sustainable ROE 12.0-13.5% vs CoE 12.0-13.5% and g 7-8%) gives Rs 188-282; the defensible intersection is Rs 240-305, whose midpoint implies 1.40x book and ~13x FY26 earnings. The load-bearing figures are FY26 PAT Rs 2,861 cr on average equity of Rs 24,084 cr (ROE 11.9%), ROA of 1.89% on average assets of Rs 151,374 cr, book value Rs 194.4/share, and the ~Rs 3,150 cr FY26 equity raise that lifted share capital from Rs 246.98 to Rs 277.91 cr and cut leverage to 6.0x. My central judgement is that the operating improvement is real — ROA has gone 1.69% to 1.89%, income has compounded at 18%, and the balance sheet is freshly capitalised — but the business still earns barely its cost of equity, which means growth creates little value and the franchise does not deserve a compounder's rating. At Rs 385.75 the stock trades at 1.98x book, which back-solves to roughly 18% sustainable ROE at a 13% CoE, or ~15% even at a generous 11.5% CoE; M&MFIN has not sustained either figure in fifteen years and has missed its own 15%-ROE target repeatedly through the cycle. I would defend Rs 240-305 to a PM as a fair band, note that a durable move to ~2.2% ROA at 6.5x leverage would justify revisiting the upper end, and call the current price REDUCE rather than AVOID because this is a sound franchise at a demanding price, not a broken one.

MANAPPURAM.method_1: Normalised-earnings multiple: rebuilt through-cycle PAT from first principles (NII ~10.4% spread on ~68,000 cr average book = ~7,100; opex ~3,200; normalised blended credit cost ~1.2% = ~840 → PAT ~2,300; band 1,900-2,600 cr) at 9-12x P/E, discounted vs pure-play gold lenders at 15-18x for the microfinance drag, gold-price cyclicality and a decade of trading 6-11x. Gives 17,100-31,200 cr equity value = Rs 182-332/share.
MANAPPURAM.method_2: Justified P/B on adjusted book: FY26 net worth 16,051 less goodwill/intangibles 88 less a 50% haircut on unprovided NNPA (4.0% of ~64,500 cr book = 2,580) → adjusted net worth ~14,700, adjusted BVPS ~Rs 157 on 93.94 cr shares. Justified P/B = (ROE-g)/(CoE-g) with sustainable ROE 15-19%, CoE ~14.5%, g ~10%, capped for the drag of 30.2% CRAR sitting idle → 1.3-1.9x → Rs 204-300/share.
MANAPPURAM.methods_are_independent: Yes. The two legs key off different sides of the accounts and move on different assumptions. Leg 1 is entirely governed by my normalisation of credit cost — the single biggest swing factor, since FY26 charged 1,585 cr (2.9% of book) vs 419 cr in FY24 — and by forward book growth; it says nothing about what the balance sheet is worth if earnings never recover. Leg 2 anchors on audited FY26 equity of 16,051 cr, which exists whether or not the microfinance book heals, and is haircut using the disclosed NNPA rather than the P&L; its multiple is driven by a long-run ROE-vs-CoE spread, not by next year's earnings. They demonstrably diverge: assume no credit normalisation at all (PAT stays ~1,000 cr) and Leg 1 collapses to roughly Rs 105-130 while Leg 2 barely moves off Rs 200+, because the over-capitalisation (CRAR 30.2% vs ~15% required, ~7,000 cr of excess equity) is real capital regardless of current profitability. Conversely a gold-price correction would cut Leg 2's asset base without immediately hitting Leg 1's spread. Their convergence at ~Rs 255 is corroboration, not arithmetic. A cash-flow leg was deliberately not used: for a lender OCF of -20,238 cr and FCF of -20,438 cr are simply loan growth funded by +23,834 cr of financing, so an FCF-yield leg would be meaningless, not independent. Likewise no EV/EBITDA leg — the reported ebitda line for this NBFC excludes finance cost from opex and is not an economic quantity.
MANAPPURAM.rationale: Manappuram is India's #2 listed gold-loan NBFC with a consolidated microfinance arm (Asirvad) that is mid-blow-up: PAT fell from 2,197 cr (FY24, 20.7% ROE) to 1,204 cr to 993 cr (FY26, 7.0% ROE) purely on credit cost, which ran 1,585 cr in FY26 (~2.9% of average book) against 419 cr in FY24, while the gold book itself boomed — total assets +51% to 74,559 cr on record bullion prices and the Bain equity infusion (share capital 169.29 → 187.87 at FV Rs 2, i.e. 84.6 → 93.94 cr shares, market cap ~34,930 cr). Leg 1 (normalised PAT 1,900-2,600 cr at 9-12x) gives Rs 182-332; Leg 2 (adjusted BVPS ~Rs 157 at justified P/B 1.3-1.9x on 15-19% sustainable ROE vs ~14.5% CoE) gives Rs 204-300; I would defend Rs 210-305, centre ~Rs 258, or ~10.5x normalised earnings and ~1.5x reported book. At 371.85 the stock trades at 35x trailing PAT and 2.18x book, which back-solves to a required sustained ROE near 20% — a level hit only at the FY24 peak on materially less capital, and now harder with CRAR at 30.2% and roughly 7,000 cr of equity yet to be levered. My central judgement is that the price already embeds a full gold-price-holds-plus-microfinance-fully-heals outcome; the bull path (FY28 PAT ~2,900 cr at 13x = ~Rs 400) is live but is the upside case, not the base case, and a 20-25% bullion correction takes fair value toward Rs 110-150, so the risk is asymmetric to the downside from here.

MASFIN.method_1: Residual-income / justified P/B anchored on reported book (Rs 2,974 cr, BVPS 161.9) with sustainable ROE 15.0-16.5% vs CoE 13.0-14.0% over a 24-year fading competitive-advantage period -> P/B 1.30-1.60x = Rs 185-260, central ~Rs 225
MASFIN.method_2: Peer-relative earnings multiple: trailing FY26 EPS of Rs 20.46 (PAT 375.82 cr / 18.37 cr shares) at 13-17x, the clearing range for Indian mid-cap MSME/diversified NBFCs of comparable growth and asset quality -> Rs 266-348, central ~Rs 307
MASFIN.methods_are_independent: Not one calculation restated. Leg 1 is an absolute spread model: its output is driven almost entirely by (sustainable ROE - CoE) and the length of the advantage period, anchored on the Rs 2,974 cr book, and it is nearly indifferent to the growth rate because at a ~2pp spread growth adds almost no value. Leg 2 is a relative model whose only inputs are trailing EPS and the multiple the market assigns comparable lenders - a pricing set in India overwhelmingly by AUM growth rate and asset quality, with no CoE in it at all. I acknowledge the identity P/B = P/E x ROE links them mechanically if both are fed the same ROE; I deliberately did not - leg 1 uses a forward re-levered ROE tested against a required return, leg 2 uses observed peer pricing on today's depressed 13.5% ROE. In practice they diverged ~35% at the midpoint (Rs 225 vs Rs 307), which is precisely the live question on this name: whether 20-25% growth financed on a thin spread, with free capital to equity of PAT - g*B = minus Rs 219 cr at 20% growth, creates value or consumes it. A P/E-vs-EV/EBITDA pairing would have been arithmetic; this pairing actually disagreed and forced a judgement.
MASFIN.rationale: Leg 1 (residual income on book): B0 = Rs 2,974.21 cr, BVPS 161.91; ROA has been pinned at 2.89 / 2.89 / 2.90% across FY24-26, so the ROE slide from 15.4% to 14.3% to 13.5% is pure de-levering (assets/equity 5.36x -> 4.68x -> 4.62x) after the equity raise, and re-levering to a historical ~5.3-5.5x restores 15-16.5% ROE; against CoE 13.0-14.0% this yields P/B 1.30-1.60x, i.e. Rs 185-260, central ~Rs 225. Leg 2 (peer P/E): trailing EPS 20.46 at 13-17x gives Rs 266-348, central ~Rs 307 - the higher answer because the market pays for the 27% revenue CAGR (Rs 979 -> 1,994 cr) and 22% PAT CAGR (Rs 206 -> 376 cr) without charging for the capital those consume. The Rs 80/share wedge is the whole case: internal capital generation is only 12.2% (ROE 13.5% x 90% retention) against 20-25% top-line growth, so growth here is structurally dilutive - the company already funded it with a QIP, and Rs 1,004 cr of the resulting cash (Rs 55/share, 17% of market cap) still sits undeployed as a further near-term ROE drag. I weight the spread model 60/40 because when ROE exceeds CoE by only ~2pp the absolute model is the more reliable guide and peer P/Es systematically over-reward NBFC growth, giving a band of Rs 215-300 (P/B 1.33-1.85x, trailing P/E 10.5-14.7x). At Rs 319.8 the stock trades at 1.98x book and 15.6x trailing - roughly 7% above my top and consistent with the market assuming a 17-18% ROE that three consecutive years of decline do not yet support; asset-quality data (GNPA/NNPA/CRAR all null in the feed) is a genuine unknown I have not been able to stress, which argues for the lower half of the band rather than the upper.

MINDACORP.method_1: Normalised earnings multiple: 20-26x on normalised PAT of Rs 290-330 cr (FY26 reported PAT 277 cr, credited with a full year of the newly-acquired 49% associate visible as the +15 cr widening of the PBT-vs-EBIT-less-interest gap). Multiple set from the business's own economics, not peer optics: an 11.4% reported ROE / ~10% normalised earnings CAGR mid-tier tier-1 supplier earns a structural-growth multiple but not a franchise one. Gives Rs 315-465/share.
MINDACORP.method_2: ROIC-constrained FCFF / value-of-invested-capital: core invested capital Rs 2,221 cr (net worth + borrowings - cash - ST investments - non-operating investments), NOPAT Rs 354 cr → ROIC 15.9%. Value/IC = (ROIC-g)/(WACC-g) across WACC 11.0-11.5% and g 7-9%, giving core EV Rs 4,440-7,780 cr; then add the Rs 1,584 cr investment portfolio at carrying value and deduct Rs 1,243 cr net debt. Gives Rs 260-441/share.
MINDACORP.methods_are_independent: Leg 1 capitalises an accounting-earnings line and is completely blind to how much cash must be ploughed back to sustain the growth embedded in that multiple. Leg 2 explicitly charges the reinvestment (g/ROIC = 44-56% of NOPAT) and separates the non-operating investment stack from the debt that bought it. They can only agree when capex converges to depreciation and leverage is stable — the opposite of this company, where capex is 1.72x D&A and borrowings went 535 → 1,609 → 1,471 cr in two years. That divergence is real, not notional: FCF conversion against PAT swung 15%, 48%, 81% and 101% across the four years, so PAT is not a fixed function of free cash here. The legs land ~60 Rs apart at their centres (390 vs 350) precisely because leg 2 makes the ramp pay for itself and leg 1 does not. Neither leg is an EV/EBITDA restatement of the other — I deliberately avoided pairing P/E with EV/EBITDA off the same FY26 column, since interest, D&A and tax are fixed there and the two would be arithmetically locked.
MINDACORP.rationale: Leg 1 (20-26x normalised PAT of 290-330 cr) gives Rs 315-465; leg 2 (ROIC 15.9%, WACC 11.0-11.5%, g 7-9% on core IC of 2,221 cr, plus 1,584 cr investments less 1,243 cr net debt) gives Rs 260-441; the honest intersection is Rs 320-440, centre ~Rs 380. The operating business is genuinely improving — revenue 6,185 cr (+22%), EBITDA margin up four straight years from 10.9% to 11.6%, ROIC ~16% — but the shareholder return is not: reported ROE is 11.4%, normalised PAT has compounded at only ~9.9% against 12.9% revenue growth, and the gap is interest and depreciation from a debt-funded acquisition whose earnings have not yet arrived. At Rs 700.95 the market pays 46.5x earnings, 17.4x core EV/EBITDA and 4.9x book, which on my inputs requires perpetual ~10.7% growth at 15.9% ROIC — plausible for India but a zero-margin-of-safety assumption for a mid-tier tier-1 supplier. My band tops out at Rs 440 (30x reported earnings), so the price sits ~59% above it: I would call this a good business at an indefensible price. Caveat recorded, not baked into the band: share capital of 47.82 cr at Rs 2 face value implies 23.91 cr shares versus the 18.39 cr supplied, and the true count would make the stock dearer still, so the AVOID holds either way.

MOTHERSON.method_1: Normalised earnings multiple: EBITDA margin normalised to 9.5-10.5% (crediting the greenfield-ramp drag) on FY26 revenue 126,104 cr, less D&A 5,018 and interest 350, taxed at 26%, then haircut ~15% for minority interests (net worth 40,980 = assets minus liabilities, so it is a consolidated-including-minority figure). Attributable EPS 3.4-4.2 on 1,083.71 cr shares, at 13-17x. Multiple justified by global Tier-1 peers at 6-12x on comparable 7-9% EBITDA margins, with a premium for scale, a 1.0x net-debt/EBITDA balance sheet and non-auto (aerospace/electronics) optionality, but no franchise multiple for a sub-WACC ROIC. Range Rs 44-68.
