MOTHERSON.method_2: Sustainable free-cash-flow yield: gross cash flow (PAT + D&A) ~9,600 cr less working-capital absorption (net WC 12,424 cr = 9.9% of revenue, so ~1,240 cr/yr at 10% growth) gives sustainable OCF ~8,400 cr; less maintenance capex of 4,000-4,800 cr (gross block 75,054 is 57% depreciated, so replacement need is real) gives FCFE 3,200-4,300 cr. Capitalised at a 6.0-7.5% required yield (12.5% CoE less 5-6.5% perpetual growth). Sense-checked against reported FCF of 2,422/3,444/1,725/5,230 (4-yr avg 3,205) and an explicit 5-year FCFF DCF (11% growth tapering to 7%, margin to 9.8%, WACC 11-11.5%, terminal g 5-5.5%, plus ~6,000 cr for investments/MSWIL stake) which returns Rs 46-56. Range Rs 39-66.
MOTHERSON.methods_are_independent: Yes, and they visibly diverged on this company's own history. The earnings leg values accounting profit struck after book D&A of 5,018 cr; the cash leg charges the cash the business must actually sink — capex of 6,054 cr running 20% above D&A, plus working capital absorbing ~10% of every incremental rupee of revenue. For an acquisitive, mid-capacity-ramp supplier whose depreciation is partly goodwill/acquired-intangible driven, those two numbers are not a fixed function of each other. Motherson proves it: FY25 delivered PAT of 4,146 cr but FCF of only 1,725 cr, while FY26 delivered flat PAT (4,086 cr) alongside FCF of 5,230 cr — a 3x swing in cash on flat earnings. The legs landed ~15% apart at the centre (earnings 44-68, cash 39-66), which is corroboration rather than arithmetic restatement. I deliberately avoided pairing P/E with EV/EBITDA, which would have been one method stated twice.
MOTHERSON.rationale: Leg 1 (normalised earnings, 13-17x on minority-adjusted EPS of 3.4-4.2) gives Rs 44-68; Leg 2 (sustainable FCFE of 3,200-4,300 cr at a 6.0-7.5% required yield) gives Rs 39-66; an explicit FCFF DCF lands Rs 46-56 — I defend Rs 50-75. The economics do not support a compounder multiple: EBITDA margin has plateaued at ~9.0% (7.8/9.2/9.3/9.0 across FY23-26), post-tax ROIC is 8.8% on invested capital of 52,197 cr and incremental post-tax ROIC over FY23-26 is only ~11.8% (delta-EBIT 3,384 on delta-IC 20,763), i.e. roughly at cost of capital, so growth is close to value-neutral. FY26 is the clearest evidence — revenue +11% to 126,104 cr, yet PAT went backwards from 4,146 to 4,086 cr, with capex of 6,054 cr against D&A of 5,018 cr and 7,309 cr of acquisition goodwill on the books. At Rs 150.75 on 1,083.71 cr shares the market cap is ~1.63 lakh cr, about 47x normalised attributable earnings and ~15x EV/EBITDA for a business earning ~10% ROE; even a hard bull case (15% revenue CAGR to FY31, 11.5% EBITDA margin, 20x exit) discounts back to only ~Rs 120, so the current price requires flawless execution of a very ambitious plan just to break even. Genuine offsets — the aerospace/consumer-electronics diversification, an honest track record of turning around distressed acquisitions like SMP, and the MSWIL stake — are what keep my top end at Rs 75 rather than the Rs 46-56 the DCF alone implies.

PAISALO.method_1: Justified P/B balance-sheet anchor: (ROE-g)/(CoE-g). Sustainable ROE 15-18% (current 14.3%, credited with partial leverage normalisation from 3.5x toward 4.5-5x since ROA is a healthy 4.1%), CoE 13.5-14.5% (smallcap unsecured lender, UP/Bihar geographic concentration, no GNPA/CRAR disclosure), g 9-10% nominal. Yields 1.3x-2.0x on FY27E BVPS ~Rs 22.7 (FY26 BVPS 19.80 grown by retained earnings) = Rs 29-45.
PAISALO.method_2: Peer-relative earnings multiple on normalised EPS: 11-15x. Bottom of range reflects MFI-adjacent cyclical credit risk and the FY26 cost-to-income deterioration to 41.8% from 37.7%; top reflects genuine 4.1% ROA, 20-27% book growth and a long rural runway. Applied to FY27E EPS ~Rs 3.04 gives Rs 33-46; on trailing FY26 EPS 2.62 gives Rs 29-39. Combined Rs 30-46. Multiple range taken from listed comparable small-ticket Indian NBFCs, NOT derived from my ROE assumption.
PAISALO.methods_are_independent: They price two different things and disagree here. Leg 1 is a return-on-capital verdict: it asks only whether ROE clears CoE, and a 14-16% ROE lender against a ~14% CoE earns only a thin premium to book regardless of how fast the book grows. Leg 2 is an earnings-stream verdict: it is indifferent to book size and rewards the 20%+ AUM growth and 4.1% ROA directly, via multiples the market actually clears for similar lenders. A lender can have fast growth and low ROE (dilutive growth — Leg 2 lands far above Leg 1, which is the case here), or 25% ROE with no growth (order flips). Critically, I did NOT set the P/E range equal to justified-P/B divided by ROE — that identity is what collapses these into one method. The residual disagreement is visible in the output: Leg 2's centre implies ~1.9x book while Leg 1's centre is ~1.65x, i.e. the two legs genuinely differ on whether growth at a mediocre ROE-CoE spread creates value. That gap, not a false 4% agreement, is why the band is Rs 30-45 rather than a point.
PAISALO.rationale: Paisalo is a high-yield small-ticket rural NBFC with genuinely good unit economics — 16.3% asset yield against 9.45% cost of funds, 4.11% ROA, and total assets compounding from Rs 3,354 cr to Rs 6,300 cr in three years — but the equity return has been stuck: ROE was 14.4%, 14.0%, 14.3% in FY24/25/26 because leverage is only 3.51x and management has repeatedly funded growth with fresh equity rather than debt, so the shareholder never captures the ROA. Leg 1 (justified P/B, ROE 15-18%, CoE 13.5-14.5%, g 9-10%) gives 1.3-2.0x FY27E book of Rs 22.7 = Rs 29-45; Leg 2 (11-15x peer earnings multiple on FY27E EPS ~3.04, cross-checked on trailing EPS 2.62) gives Rs 30-46; the intersection is Rs 30-45. At Rs 71.2 the stock trades at 27.2x trailing earnings and 3.60x book, which requires roughly 21% sustainable ROE to justify on any reasonable CoE — a 50% step-up from three years of flat 14%, achievable only if leverage normalises to ~5x with no ROA erosion, which is precisely what four years of behaviour says will not happen. Two further discounts apply: the FY26 cost-to-income jump to 41.8% from 37.7% hints at rising credit cost in an unsecured rural book during a stressed microfinance cycle, and the payload carries no GNPA/NNPA/CRAR at all, so the asset quality underwriting this multiple is unverifiable. I would defend Rs 30-45 to a PM as fair value and call the current price a growth-narrative premium rather than intrinsic value.

PIRAMALFIN.method_1: Normalised earnings multiple. FY26 PBT Rs 1,383 cr taxed at a normal 25% gives normalised PAT ~Rs 1,037 cr / EPS Rs 45.5 (reported PAT Rs 1,506 cr is flattered by a Rs 123 cr tax CREDIT off FY23 loss carry-forwards, so reported EPS 66.1 overstates run-rate earnings power). FY27E normalised EPS Rs 75-92 assuming 15-18% book growth continues with opex leverage as the retail book seasons. Multiple 15-20x forward (discount to Chola/Bajaj Finance for the FY23 wholesale wipeout and unproven through-cycle credit costs on a used-car/MSME/unsecured-heavy mix; premium to LIC Housing for growth and capital strength), equivalently 25-30x on trough trailing earnings. Range Rs 1,150-1,600, centre ~Rs 1,290.
PIRAMALFIN.method_2: Adjusted-book / excess-capital SOTP using justified P/B = (ROE-g)/(CoE-g). Split the Rs 28,148.66 cr net worth: operating equity at a normal 17% equity/assets = Rs 18,793 cr, valued at 0.6-1.1x on sustainable ROE 11-14.5%, g 8-9%, CoE 13.5% (Rs 11,276-20,672 cr); PLUS Rs 9,355 cr of surplus capital (the gap between actual 25.5% equity/assets and a normal 17%) at 0.85-1.0x book (Rs 7,952-9,355 cr); LESS Rs ~1,660 cr for goodwill Rs 2 cr + intangibles Rs 258 cr and a 5% haircut for residual Wholesale-1.0/AIF legacy exposure and deferred-tax-asset quality. Total Rs 17,568-28,367 cr, i.e. Rs 770-1,245/share, centre ~Rs 1,010 (0.62-1.01x reported book). Independent cross-check on the same balance-sheet frame: book compounding ~10% to Rs 39-41k cr by FY30, exit 1.0-1.3x P/B, discounted 4 years at 13.5% = Rs 1,030-1,415.
PIRAMALFIN.methods_are_independent: First, cash-flow legs are unusable here: operating CF of -Rs 15,892 cr (FY26) and -Rs 8,119 cr (FY25) are simply loan disbursements under Ind AS, not economic cash burn, so FCF yield is meaningless for a lender. The two legs I used are an EARNINGS leg and a BALANCE-SHEET leg, and they can and did diverge sharply (centres Rs 1,290 vs Rs 1,010, a 28% gap, overlapping only in Rs 1,150-1,245). They diverge for two structural reasons. (1) Leg 2 credits Rs 9,355 cr of surplus capital that contributes essentially NOTHING to Leg 1: the company runs 3.9x leverage / 25.5% equity-to-assets against a normal ~5.9x, so that idle equity is invisible in the current P&L run-rate that Leg 1 capitalises, but is real deployable book value in Leg 2. (2) Conversely, Leg 2 penalises a sustainable ROE that sits BELOW the cost of equity with a sub-1x justified book multiple (13% ROE vs 13.5% CoE gives 0.89x), a value-destruction signal that Leg 1's growth-driven P/E ignores entirely - a 30%-growth earnings trajectory can carry 25-30x regardless of whether the returns clear CoE. So the legs answer different questions (what is the profit stream worth vs what is the equity base worth) and would agree only by coincidence. Note the residual link - P/B = P/E x ROE - is broken here because Leg 1 uses the CURRENT depressed 3.7% normalised ROE while Leg 2 uses a mid-cycle 11-14.5% ROE on a re-levered balance sheet; the 3-4x gap between those ROEs is precisely the axis of disagreement.
PIRAMALFIN.rationale: Piramal Finance is a post-blow-up NBFC two years into a retail turnaround: PAT swung from -Rs 7,401 cr (FY23) to +Rs 485 cr (FY25) to +Rs 1,506 cr (FY26) on revenue of Rs 11,852 cr, total assets up 16% to Rs 110,546 cr and net worth Rs 28,149 cr - but FY26 ROA is only 1.47% and ROE 5.4% (1.0% and 3.7% on a normalised 25% tax rate, since reported PAT is flattered by a Rs 123 cr tax credit off FY23 loss carry-forwards), and the balance sheet is over-capitalised at 25.5% equity/assets, i.e. 3.9x leverage against a normal ~5.9x. Leg 1 (normalised EPS Rs 45.5 trailing / Rs 75-92 FY27E, at 15-20x forward or 25-30x trough) gives Rs 1,150-1,600; Leg 2 (0.6-1.1x justified P/B on 11-14.5% sustainable ROE vs 13.5% CoE applied to Rs 18,793 cr operating equity, plus Rs 9,355 cr surplus capital at 0.85-1.0x, less Rs 1.66k cr for intangibles and legacy-wholesale/DTA quality) gives Rs 770-1,245, and a four-year re-levering path (book to Rs 39-41k cr by FY30, exit 1.0-1.3x, discounted at 13.5%) independently brackets Rs 1,030-1,415. I defend Rs 1,050-1,420, centred near Rs 1,225 or roughly 1.0x current book - the re-levering that drives ROE up is genuinely happening organically (equity/assets fell 28.5% to 25.5% in FY26), but it takes four-plus years of sub-10% ROE to get there and the credit costs on a used-car/MSME/unsecured-heavy book are unproven through a cycle. At Rs 2,055.5 the stock trades at 1.66x book and 31x reported (45x normalised) earnings, which is exactly the justified P/B for a fully-arrived 15% ROE with 10% perpetual growth - the terminal state, priced as if it were already here, by a management team that wrote off Rs 7,400 cr in FY23 and is earning 5% ROE today. Price sits ~45% above the top of my band, hence AVOID.

PNBHOUSING.method_1: Residual-income / justified P/B balance-sheet anchor. FY26 net worth Rs 19,219 cr on 26.1 cr shares = BVPS Rs 736; accreted ~4 months into FY27 at 12% book growth = current BVPS ~Rs 769. Sustainable ROE 12.5-14.5% (trailing 12.7%, with upside from leverage normalising off an unusually low 4.87x assets/equity and mix shift to higher-yield affordable, capped by a thin 1.58% spread: 9.06% pre-interest pre-tax return on assets vs 7.48% cost of debt). CoE 12.75% (rf 6.5% + beta ~1.15 x ERP 5.5%), g 8.5%. Justified P/B = (ROE-g)/(CoE-g) = 0.94x bear / 1.18x base / 1.41x bull, cross-checked with a 5-year two-stage RI build (ROE ramping 13.0%->14.5%, 10% payout) which lands ~1.10x. Range Rs 725-1,085, central ~Rs 905.
PNBHOUSING.method_2: Peer-relative earnings multiple on credit-cost-normalised earnings. FY26 reported PAT Rs 2,291 cr = EPS Rs 87.8 (trailing P/E 12.0x). Haircut ~7% for a normalised credit cost of ~30-35bp of average assets (recent P&L carries near-zero/negative credit cost from legacy written-off-pool recoveries, which are finite) -> recurring EPS ~Rs 82. Multiple 11-15x, central 13x: above the LIC HF / Repco tier (6-7x) on PAT growth of 18% and a repaired retail book, below Can Fin (~12x at 18% ROE) and well below the affordable-HFC premium names (Aavas/Home First 22-25x) on inferior ROE, no cost-of-funds advantage, and chronic balance-transfer attrition in prime. Range Rs 900-1,230, central ~Rs 1,065.
PNBHOUSING.methods_are_independent: Cash-flow legs are structurally unusable here: FY26 OCF is -Rs 8,984 cr and FCF -Rs 9,017 cr purely because loan disbursement is an operating item for an HFC, so FCF yield carries no valuation information. The two legs I used diverge for a real reason. Leg 1 is an absolute-return judgement: its output is almost entirely a function of the ROE-minus-CoE spread and the (CoE - g) denominator, and it is indifferent to what peers trade at. Leg 2 is a market-relative judgement anchored on delivered rupees of profit and where HFC peers' earnings multiples sit, and it is indifferent to CoE and terminal growth. They are not the same equation restated: a 100bp change in CoE moves Leg 1 by roughly 25% and Leg 2 by zero; a 30bp change in normalised credit cost moves Leg 2 by ~10% and Leg 1 barely at all. Empirically they did disagree here, by ~17% at the centre (Rs 905 vs Rs 1,065) and their bands only overlap over Rs 900-1,085 - Leg 1 penalises PNBHF for earning barely its cost of equity, Leg 2 rewards it for 18% PAT growth and a cleaned-up book. Residual linkage (P/B = P/E x ROE) exists for any lender, but the legs use different ROE vintages (medium-term sustainable vs credit-normalised trailing) and different discipline sources, so they are genuinely capable of contradiction.
PNBHOUSING.rationale: PNB Housing is a repaired but not yet franchise-grade mortgage lender: FY26 PAT Rs 2,291 cr (+18%, decelerating from +44%/+28%), assets Rs 93,512 cr (+13.3%), ROE 12.70% and ROA 2.60%, trading at Rs 1,053 for a Rs 27,486 cr market cap = 1.43x FY26 book (BVPS Rs 736) and 12.0x reported EPS of Rs 87.8. The central tension is that ROA is flattered by an unusually unlevered balance sheet - assets/equity of only 4.87x means roughly a fifth of the book is equity-funded - so ROE sits at barely its cost of equity today, while the same surplus capital is the main reason ROE can climb to ~14% by FY29 without dilution as leverage normalises toward 6x and the affordable book scales. Balance-sheet leg (justified P/B 0.94-1.41x on sustainable ROE 12.5-14.5% vs CoE 12.75%, g 8.5%, applied to current BVPS ~Rs 769) gives Rs 725-1,085; earnings leg (11-15x on credit-cost-normalised EPS ~Rs 82, since recent credit cost is near zero on finite legacy recoveries) gives Rs 900-1,230. I would defend Rs 850-1,080, weighting the book leg slightly more because for a spread lender the ROE-vs-CoE gap is what actually determines value and a 1.4x multiple implicitly demands a sustained 15%+ ROE that the 1.58% asset spread does not support. At Rs 1,053 the stock sits inside but in the upper third of that band - fairly valued to slightly full, with no margin of safety; genuine downside to ~Rs 615 if affordable-book credit costs season to 1%+, genuine upside to ~Rs 1,350 if ROE reaches 16%.

POONAWALLA.method_1: Forward normalised earnings power: FY28 average assets ~Rs 88,150 cr (30% then 25% asset growth off the Rs 60,272 cr FY26 base) x normalised post-tax ROA of 1.4%/1.8%/2.3% = PAT Rs 1,234/1,587/2,027 cr; ~86 cr shares after the equity raise needed to hold 6.5x leverage; EPS Rs 14.3/18.4/23.6; exit P/E 16x/18x/20x (a 20-25% grower with mid-teens ROE, capped for execution/governance risk); discounted 2 yrs at 13.5% CoE = Rs 178 / 258 / 366 per share. Range Rs 178-366, central ~Rs 257.
POONAWALLA.method_2: Balance-sheet anchor on DEMONSTRATED returns: BVPS Rs 130.26 (net worth Rs 10,348.24 cr / 79.44 cr sh). Delivered ROE is 8.6% FY23, ~9-10% FY24 ex the subsidiary-sale gain, -1.2% FY25, 5.9% FY26 — a ~6% four-year average. Granting through-cycle sustainable ROE of only 10-14%, the Indian NBFC P/B-vs-ROE ladder (LTF/M&M Fin ~1.6-1.7x at 11-12% ROE; Shriram ~2.0x at 16%; Chola ~4.5x at 20%) gives 1.5-2.3x book = Rs 195-300, central ~Rs 195 at 1.5x. Cross-checked with an explicit 5-yr residual-income run at CoE 13.5% on an OPTIMISTIC ROE path (8%→11%→13%→14%→14%, terminal spread 50bp): PV of RI -Rs 677 cr + terminal Rs 833 cr = equity Rs 10,505 cr = Rs 132/sh, i.e. the strict excess-return math says roughly book and argues for the low end. Stressed tangible book (less Rs 33 cr intangibles, less 1.5-2% latent credit on the ~Rs 55,000 cr loan book) = Rs 116-120/sh floor.
POONAWALLA.methods_are_independent: Yes, structurally. Leg 1 values a P&L two years out — it multiplies a forecast asset base by an assumed steady-state ROA and an exit P/E, so it fully credits the build-out (opex is running at 4.26% of assets vs a 3.0-3.4% mature level, which is the entire bull case). Leg 2 never uses that forecast: it anchors on today's Rs 10,348 cr equity and pays only for returns the company has actually delivered, charging a full 13.5% CoE against the equity that growth is consuming. They diverge because they embed opposite views of the same unknown — Leg 1 assumes ROE roughly triples from 5.85% to 14-16%, Leg 2 pays for ~10-12%. They did not agree mechanically: Leg 1's central Rs 257 is ~32% above Leg 2's central Rs 195, and the RI cross-check inside Leg 2 lands at Rs 132, half of Leg 1's centre. Different denominators too (assets x ROA x P/E vs equity x P/B), so neither is a restatement of the other. Note: EV/EBITDA and FCF are meaningless here — operating cash flow is -Rs 21,786 cr purely because the loan book nearly doubled, and "interest expense" of Rs 221 cr excludes the Rs 2,767 cr of finance cost sitting in cost of revenue.
POONAWALLA.rationale: Poonawalla Fincorp is a wholesale-funded, promoter-backed NBFC in the middle of a second aggressive rebuild: total assets went Rs 34,945 cr → Rs 60,272 cr (+72.5%) in FY26 and revenue Rs 3,989 cr → Rs 6,463 cr, but FY26 PAT was only Rs 541.81 cr — ROE 5.85%, ROA 1.14%, after an outright loss of Rs 98 cr in FY25 when the prior high-yield book was written down. Net total income is a healthy 7.76% of average assets, but 4.26% goes to opex (build-out) and ~1.98% to credit costs, so the earnings power is real only if both normalise. Leg 1 (normalised FY28 earnings, ROA 1.4-2.3%, 16-20x, discounted back) gives Rs 178-366; Leg 2 (P/B 1.5-2.3x on Rs 130.26 BVPS against 10-14% demonstrated-plus-improvement ROE) gives Rs 195-300, with a strict residual-income run at 13.5% CoE landing near book at Rs 132 and a stressed tangible-book floor of Rs 116-120. I would defend Rs 200-320 (roughly 1.5-2.5x book, ~14-19x normalised EPS), centred ~Rs 250. At Rs 463.55 the market is paying 3.56x book and 68x trailing earnings, which requires flawless execution to ~2.2%+ ROA on a Rs 130,000 cr book by FY29 — and a loan book that grew 72% in one year in high-yield segments, at a lender that has already had one credit blow-up, is exactly where I would not underwrite that; 45% above my ceiling with no margin of safety.

PRICOLLTD.method_1: Normalised earnings multiple: 18-26x clean FY26 PAT of Rs 250 cr (PBT 330.94 less tax 80.14, no exceptional item), a 30-35% discount to quality Indian auto-ancillary comps for cyclical 2W end-market dependence, OEM customer concentration, 12% EBITDA margins with limited pricing power, and equity destroyed as recently as FY24 (reserves were negative Rs 204 cr in FY23). Gives Rs 4,500-6,500 cr equity = Rs 369-533/sh.
PRICOLLTD.method_2: Owner cash earnings capitalised: PAT 250 + D&A 120 - maintenance capex ~140 (D&A plus inflation on a growing gross block of 1,639.73) - normalised working-capital absorption ~70 (NWC is 14.5% of sales, ~53 days, so ~2% of sales consumed annually at trend growth) = Rs 160 cr. Capitalised at a required yield of 4.0-5.0% (CoE 12-12.5% less sustainable growth 8-9%) = Rs 3,200-4,000 cr equity = Rs 262-328/sh.
PRICOLLTD.methods_are_independent: Leg 1 is an accrual-earnings multiple; Leg 2 is a cash measure built from OCF-equivalent less maintenance capex less working-capital absorption. They are not arithmetic restatements of each other because Pricol converts only ~55-65% of accounting profit into owner cash: capex is running at 2.7x depreciation (323.4 vs 119.7 in FY26) and working capital absorbs roughly 2% of sales a year. Over FY23-26 cumulative reported FCF was Rs 240 cr against cumulative PAT of Rs 683 cr, i.e. 35% conversion, and FY26 FCF was actually NEGATIVE Rs 42 cr in the same year PAT hit a record Rs 250.8 cr. The earnings leg sees a 22%-ROE compounder; the cash leg sees a business that has returned essentially nothing to owners while it builds capacity. The legs in fact FAILED to overlap (369-533 vs 262-328), which is the divergence proving independence - if capex normalised to maintenance levels they would converge, and I reconciled them 60/40 toward earnings because incremental ROIC of ~23% means the growth capex is genuinely productive and a static cash yield over-penalises it. I deliberately avoided a P/E vs EV/EBITDA pair, which for this company would have been one method restated (EBITDA 491.83 less D&A 119.7 less interest 45.99 less 24% tax mechanically reproduces PAT 250.8).
PRICOLLTD.rationale: Pricol is a genuinely improved 2W-levered Tier-1 (instrument clusters, sensors, pumps): FY23-26 revenue 1,958.6 to 4,040.8, EBITDA margin stable at 11.8-12.4%, PAT 124.7 to 250.8, ROE 22.1% on average equity of 1,135 and post-tax ROIC ~22% on average invested capital of 1,270 - but reserves were negative Rs 204 cr as recently as FY23, so this is a completed turnaround rather than a proven long-run franchise, and FY26's ~50% revenue step was part-inorganic with borrowings rising 134.7 to 379.2. The earnings leg at 18-26x normalised PAT of 250 gives Rs 369-533; the owner-cash leg (160 cr of cash earnings at a 4.0-5.0% required yield) gives Rs 262-328; reconciling 60/40 toward earnings gives a defended band of Rs 330-455, corroborated by an independent 7-year/15%-growth/22%-ROIC/12%-WACC DCF at Rs 332, a generous 8%-terminal/11%-WACC version at Rs 532, and a justified P/B of 2.9-4.0x giving Rs 299-412. At Rs 696.65 the market cap is Rs 8,492 cr (EV 8,743) = 33.9x earnings, 17.8x EV/EBITDA and 6.8x book, which on (ROE-g)/(CoE-g) requires roughly 11% perpetual growth from a cyclical component supplier that has not yet generated free cash. My central judgement is that the operating improvement is real and the returns on incremental capital are good, but the price capitalises a decade of uninterrupted execution at a moment when the company is burning cash to fund it - I would not own it above ~Rs 455 and the band top already assumes the bullish end of the multiple range.

SBFC.method_1: Comp-anchored P/E on normalised one-year-forward EPS. FY26 EPS Rs 4.10; normalising credit cost to a through-cycle ~1.5% of assets trims FY26 to ~Rs 4.00, and FY27E on ~25% AUM growth with ~1.5pp further cost/income improvement gives EPS ~Rs 5.10. Multiple range 14-18x forward: a 25-30% grower with real collateral (residential LAP, ~45-50% LTV) and best-in-class 4.6% ROA earns the top of the secured-retail-NBFC comp set (Aptus, Home First, Five Star, Can Fin trade ~11-22x), but a sub-CoE 13% ROE, only three years of listed history, an unseasoned book and a credit cost that has trebled in three years cap it well short of a franchise multiple. Range: Rs 71-92.
SBFC.method_2: Balance-sheet anchor: ten-year residual-income build on reported book, cross-checked against justified P/B = (ROE-g)/(CoE-g). Book Rs 3,725 cr (BVPS Rs 33.88; TBVPS Rs 31.45 after Rs 260 cr goodwill). Sustainable ROE derived from a driver model back-solved to reproduce the actual 13.0% (yield 17.0%, CoF 8.62%, opex 4.12%, credit cost 1.35%): 13% if leverage stays ~3.5x, ~16% at 4.25x, ~19% at 4.75x - so ROE path peaks 15.5-19%, terminal 15-16%. CoE 13.25-14.25% (Rs 10k cr mid-cap NBFC, credit-cyclical, untested through a downturn, beta ~1.2), terminal g 9-10%. Yields 1.4-2.4x book. Range: Rs 48-80 (central Rs 60 at CoE 13.75%, peak ROE 17.5%).
SBFC.methods_are_independent: They price two different things and here they genuinely conflict. The P/E leg capitalises near-term reported earnings at a multiple observed in the market - it is agnostic to how much equity is standing behind those earnings, so it happily pays 22x for a business whose ROE is 13%. The RI/justified-P/B leg does the opposite: it charges a full 13.25-14.25% cost of equity against the Rs 3,725 cr book every year and only pays for the spread earned above it. For SBFC that spread is currently NEGATIVE (ROE 13.0% < CoE ~13.75%) because the company is under-levered at 3.0x assets/equity, so the book leg lands far below the earnings leg (Rs 48-80 vs Rs 71-92) and they overlap only at Rs 71-80. The wedge is the leverage-up assumption, and the two legs move in opposite directions on it: raising leverage lifts ROE and the book leg, but compresses NIM/assets and would flatter neither leg identically. They would also diverge on credit-cost normalisation (hits the earnings leg immediately, the book leg only through terminal ROE) and on de-rating of the comp set (moves leg 1 alone). This is not P/E and EV/EBITDA restated - EV multiples are inapplicable to a lender and no cash-flow leg exists here, since OCF is -Rs 1,893 cr purely because loan-book growth is classified as operating.
SBFC.rationale: SBFC is a small-ticket secured MSME/LAP lender: FY26 total income Rs 1,679 cr, PAT Rs 450.8 cr (EPS Rs 4.10), net worth Rs 3,725 cr (BVPS Rs 33.88), assets Rs 11,085 cr - so at Rs 90.4 it trades on 22.1x trailing earnings and 2.67x book (2.87x tangible). The underlying economics are genuinely good (ROA 4.58%, NII/assets 11.6%, cost/income compressed 47%-to-34% in three years, 44% PAT CAGR), but ROE is only 13.0% because leverage is just 3.0x assets/equity, and my back-solved driver model says sustainable ROE is ~13% if that under-leverage persists and 16-19% only if they push leverage to 4.25-4.75x - all while implied credit cost has trebled from 0.51% to 1.35% of assets. Leg 1 (14-18x normalised FY27E EPS of ~Rs 5.10) gives Rs 71-92; leg 2 (ten-year residual income on Rs 3,725 cr book, CoE 13.25-14.25%, peak ROE 15.5-19%, terminal g 9-10%) gives 1.4-2.4x book, or Rs 48-80. They intersect only at Rs 71-80, which I regard as false precision, so I defend Rs 62-88 with the centre (~Rs 74; 2.2x book, 14.5x forward) sitting inside that overlap. At Rs 90.4 the market is already capitalising an ROE the company has not yet earned, with credit quality actively deteriorating and no evidence yet that management intends to lever up - REDUCE, price above the top of my band and ~21% above centre.

SHRIPISTON.method_1: Normalised earnings multiple: P/E 20-26x on normalised PAT of ~Rs 575 cr (FY26 PAT 561.4 annualised for the acquisition and charged a full year of interest on the new Rs 1,968 cr borrowings, ~95 cr post-tax drag). Multiple set at 20-26x: above the auto-ancillary median for a domestic leader with a sticky high-margin aftermarket and 21% ROE, but below franchise multiples for ICE-powertrain terminal risk, auto cyclicality, decelerating organic growth (FY26 PAT +8.9% vs revenue +25.6%) and goodwill-heavy M&A. Gives Rs 2,570-3,340/share; EV/EBITDA cross-check at 12-18x on FY26 EBITDA 852.75 less net debt 938.9 gives Rs 2,075-3,218.
SHRIPISTON.method_2: Cash-flow value: reinvestment-linked FCFF DCF plus an FCF-yield cross-check. NOPAT 526.7 (EBIT 704.15 at 25.2% cash tax); normalised capex ~5.3% of sales (235) plus ~80 cr/yr working-capital absorption less D&A 148.6 gives a ~32% reinvestment rate and steady-state FCFF ~361 cr. Ten-year model (12% growth for 5 yrs, incremental ROIC 20% fading to 15%, terminal 5-6%) at WACC 10.5-11.8% gives EV 6,784-9,590, equity Rs 1,305-1,931/share. FCF-yield check: OCF 625.05 less normalised capex 235 = ~390 cr FCFE at a generous 3.5-5.0% yield gives Rs 1,741-2,480. Justified P/B on 21% sustainable ROE (2.8-4.3x on book/share 647.6) independently lands 1,813-2,806. Leg range ~Rs 1,700-2,400.
SHRIPISTON.methods_are_independent: They can and do diverge sharply here (leg 1 midpoint ~2,950 vs leg 2 midpoint ~2,050, a 44% gap), because three things break the PAT-to-cash link in this specific business. (1) The FY26 acquisition was funded with ~Rs 1,460 cr of debt raised so late in the year that interest expense actually FELL (64.94 to 39.81) while borrowings tripled - an earnings multiple applied to reported PAT capitalises a cost base that has not yet arrived, whereas the DCF charges the full capital deployed against the returns it earns. (2) Cash conversion is volatile and structurally below PAT: in FY25 PAT rose 17.5% while OCF FELL 10.7% (486.7 to 434.4), because receivables and inventory absorb ~18% of sales and capex (191) runs above D&A (149). A multiple leg is blind to that; a cash-flow leg is driven by it. (3) The multiple leg is a relative-market judgement (what peers fetch), while the DCF is an absolute discount-rate/terminal-fade judgement - the ICE-displacement fade assumption moves leg 2 by 50% and does not touch leg 1 at all. This is NOT the P/E-vs-EV/EBITDA trap: those would be arithmetic restatements of the same year's income statement, and indeed my EV/EBITDA figure (2,075-3,218) sits inside leg 1 as a same-family check rather than as a second leg.
SHRIPISTON.rationale: Leading Indian ICE-powertrain component maker (pistons, rings, valves) with a genuine aftermarket franchise: revenue 2,609 to 4,459 cr over three years (19.5% CAGR), EBITDA margin 19-21%, ROE 21.2%, ROIC ex-goodwill ~21%. But FY26 is a turn: PAT grew only 8.9% on 25.6% revenue growth, margin slipped to 19.1%, and a debt-funded acquisition put goodwill at 1,323 cr and borrowings at 1,968 cr, dropping post-goodwill ROIC to ~13.7% - barely above cost of capital - while its full interest cost is still absent from reported earnings. Earnings leg (20-26x on ~575 cr normalised PAT) gives Rs 2,570-3,340; cash-flow leg (FCFF DCF at ~32% reinvestment, WACC 10.5-11.8%, plus a 3.5-5.0% FCF yield on ~390 cr FCFE, corroborated by justified P/B of 2.8-4.3x on book of 647.6) gives Rs 1,700-2,400. The legs do not overlap, so I bridge them at Rs 2,100-2,900, central ~2,500 - about 20x normalised earnings, 15x EV/EBITDA and 3.9x book on 21% ROE, all internally coherent. At 4,395 (35x trailing, 24x EV/EBITDA, 6.8x book) the market is implying roughly 10.4% growth in perpetuity at 20% ROIC, i.e. nominal-GDP growth forever for a business facing structural ICE displacement and a just-levered balance sheet, so the price sits ~50% above the top of my band.

SONACOMS.method_1: Normalised-earnings multiple: FY26 PAT Rs 629.2 cr on 61.09 cr shares = EPS Rs 10.30; normalised to ~Rs 10.5 by lifting EBITDA margin from the compressed 23.2% back toward a 24% mid-cycle level on FY26 revenue of Rs 4,449 cr. Applied 22-32x. The multiple is set above the Indian auto-ancillary median because the franchise is real — 43.9% gross margin, 23-27% EBITDA margin, ex-goodwill ROIC of 18.1%, and 18.8% three-year revenue CAGR with EV/driveline content optionality — but well below the 45-60x India has historically paid for this name, because headline ROE has fallen to 10.5%, PAT grew only 4.9% in FY26, and EBITDA margin has compressed 420bps in two years (27.4% FY24 to 23.2% FY26). Range: Rs 231-336, call it Rs 230-335.
SONACOMS.method_2: Cash-flow leg: two-stage FCFF DCF off owner earnings, cross-checked with a justified P/B. FY26 OCF Rs 659.1 cr less capex Rs 491.8 cr = FCF Rs 167.2 cr; four-year average FCF is only Rs 274 cr on a business whose revenue rose 68% over the same span, so cash generation is flat while PAT rose 59%. DCF: 15% revenue growth for 3 years then 10% for 3, EBIT margin recovering 16.7% to 18.0%, 25.2% tax, incremental sales/capital 1.5-2.0, WACC 11.0-12.0%, terminal growth 6.0-6.5% at terminal ROIC 14-18%, plus net cash of Rs 804.6 cr. Output spans Rs 142-211/share across that grid. Justified P/B = (ROE-g)/(CoE-g) on book value of Rs 97.9/share with sustainable ROE 16-18%, CoE 12%, g 6-8% gives 1.67-2.50x = Rs 163-245. Combined cash-flow/balance-sheet leg: Rs 150-230.
SONACOMS.methods_are_independent: They diverge because one capitalises accrual profit and the other charges the cash the growth actually consumes. Leg 1 stops at PAT, which excludes growth capex and working-capital absorption entirely. Leg 2 charges both in full — and for this business those are enormous right now: capex of Rs 491.8 cr is 1.71x D&A of Rs 287.7 cr, and FY26 saw a working-capital build of roughly Rs 580 cr (receivables Rs 703 to Rs 1,149 cr, inventory Rs 377 to Rs 659 cr) as the acquired railway business consolidated. The result is a 3.8x gap between PAT (Rs 629 cr) and FCF (Rs 167 cr), and the two legs landed roughly 50% apart (Rs 230-335 vs Rs 150-230) rather than agreeing — which is the proof they are not one method restated. The balance-sheet cross-check inside leg 2 is independently informative too: the Rs 1,943 cr FY25 equity raise plus roughly Rs 1,050 cr of goodwill/intangibles added in FY26 cut ROE from 19.5% to 10.5%, a fact the P/E leg is blind to. I deliberately did NOT use EV/EBITDA as a leg — at a 25.2% tax rate and Rs 288 cr of D&A it is a near-deterministic restatement of the P/E leg. I ran it only as a sanity check (12-18x gives Rs 216-317) and let it inform the band width, not the band centre.
SONACOMS.rationale: Leg 1 (22-32x normalised EPS of Rs 10.5) gives Rs 230-335; leg 2 (FCFF DCF Rs 142-211, justified P/B 1.67-2.50x on book of Rs 97.9 giving Rs 163-245) gives Rs 150-230. Key figures: FY26 revenue Rs 4,449.5 cr (+25.5%, partly acquisition-fed), EBITDA Rs 1,030.3 cr at a 23.2% margin down from 27.4% in FY24, PAT Rs 629.2 cr (+4.9% only), of which roughly Rs 201 cr of pre-tax other income comes off the cash pile rather than operations; ROE 10.5%, ROIC 10.7% headline but 18.1% ex-goodwill; FCF Rs 167 cr against capex at 1.71x D&A. My judgement is that this is a genuinely high-quality auto-ancillary franchise whose returns have been temporarily diluted by a large equity raise and an expensive railway-division acquisition, so I weight leg 1 slightly higher and settle on Rs 210-330 — the top end already assumes margins recover to 25%+ and the market keeps paying a ~28x multiple two years out. At Rs 769.4 the stock trades at 74.7x trailing earnings, 44.8x EV/EBITDA, 7.9x book and a 0.36% FCF yield on a 10.5% ROE with mid-single-digit earnings growth; that is 2.3x my band ceiling, and no defensible combination of margin recovery and terminal assumptions closes that gap, hence AVOID.

SUNDARMFIN.method_1: EARNINGS-POWER MULTIPLE. FY26 PAT Rs 2,005.4 cr / 10.73 cr shares = EPS Rs 186.90. Decomposing FY26: gross income Rs 9,668 cr on avg assets Rs 80,566 cr = 12.0% yield; implied finance cost Rs 4,872 cr leaves net income Rs 4,797 cr = 5.95% of assets; opex (SGA + depreciation) Rs 1,692 cr = 2.1%; residual implied credit cost Rs 629 cr = 0.78% of assets (~0.9% of loans) — very low, confirming top-decile underwriting in vehicle finance. ROA 2.49%, stable in a 2.36-2.60% band over three years; PAT CAGR 16.1% and book CAGR 14.5% FY23-26; asset growth 13.9%. This is a durable franchise, not a commodity lender, so it earns a premium multiple — but a 14-15% ROE does not earn a Bajaj/Chola multiple (those rest on 18-22% ROEs), and it clearly deserves more than the 12-16x that mid-quality vehicle financiers carry. Fair range 17-23x FY26 EPS, with the top end crediting the consolidated AMC, home-finance and general-insurance subsidiaries. Range: Rs 3,177 - 4,299 (mid ~20x = Rs 3,738).
SUNDARMFIN.method_2: BALANCE-SHEET ANCHOR — residual income / justified P/B. Book Rs 14,893.65 cr = BVPS Rs 1,388.0. Measured ROE 14.28% FY26 (13.55/14.94/14.28 over FY24-26, very stable), on conservative leverage of only 5.74x avg assets/avg equity. Payout 20.3% (dividend Rs 408 cr), so internally funded growth = 14.28% x 79.7% = 11.4%, matching the observed 14.5% book CAGR. Ten-year explicit RI stage then terminal g 8%: at ROE 14.5% / CoE 12.5% value is Rs 1,768 (1.27x book); at ROE 16.0% (leverage normalising toward 6.5x) / CoE 11.0% value is Rs 3,420 (2.46x book). Single-stage cross-check (ROE-g)/(CoE-g) gives 1.20-2.40x book = Rs 1,666-3,331. Raw RI range Rs 1,768-3,420. Adding an explicit SOTP uplift of Rs 350-450/share for Sundaram AMC and the general-insurance stake, whose franchise value exceeds both the equity they carry and their earnings contribution, gives Rs 2,118 - 3,870 (central ~Rs 3,000).
SUNDARMFIN.methods_are_independent: Yes, and here they actively fight. Leg 1's output is a function of earnings power and a franchise-quality multiple; it is completely indifferent to whether ROE clears the cost of equity. Leg 2's output is a function of the (ROE - CoE) spread, the reinvestment rate and terminal growth; it is completely indifferent to what any other NBFC trades at. The P/B = P/E x ROE identity links observed multiples, not these two estimation procedures — neither leg consumes the other's input. They could easily have agreed: if ROE were 21% against a 12% CoE, justified P/B would be ~4.3x, implying ~20x P/E, landing exactly on Leg 1. They do not agree here. The earnings leg says a 16%-CAGR compounder with ~0.9% credit cost is worth ~20x (2.7x book); the balance-sheet leg says a 14.3% ROE against an 11-12.5% CoE only earns 1.3-2.5x book even after crediting the subsidiaries. That ~1,000/share gap IS the finding and is why my band sits below the market price. I deliberately did NOT build an FCF leg: operating cash flow is structurally and deeply negative every year (-Rs 5,892 cr FY26, -Rs 8,985 cr FY25) because loan disbursements run through operating cash for a lender, so an FCF-yield leg would be meaningless, and EV/EBITDA is both unavailable and mechanically chained to P/E.
SUNDARMFIN.rationale: Sundaram Finance is a genuinely high-quality, conservatively run vehicle-finance NBFC with a deposit franchise and consolidated AMC/home-finance/general-insurance arms: FY26 PAT Rs 2,005 cr (EPS 186.9), net worth Rs 14,894 cr (BVPS 1,388), ROA 2.49%, ROE 14.28%, leverage only 5.74x, implied credit cost ~0.78% of assets, PAT compounding 16.1% and book 14.5% over three years. Leg 1 (17-23x FY26 EPS) gives Rs 3,177-4,299; Leg 2 (10-year residual income at ROE 14.5-16.0%, CoE 11.0-12.5%, terminal g 8%, plus Rs 350-450 of subsidiary SOTP uplift) gives Rs 2,118-3,870 — the legs overlap only at Rs 3,177-3,870, and I widen modestly around that to Rs 3,050-4,150 (16.3-22.2x, 2.20-2.99x book) to reflect the genuine method disagreement. My central judgement is that the market is paying 24.96x earnings and 3.36x book for a 14.3% ROE, and no defensible cost of equity for an Indian NBFC (11%+) supports that from the balance sheet — the quality premium is real but is already more than fully capitalised, and the low leverage that makes the franchise safe is the same thing that caps ROE. At Rs 4,665.6 the price sits 12% above the top of my band and 30% above the midpoint, so REDUCE rather than AVOID: the business is excellent and a year of 15% compounding closes part of the gap, but there is no margin of safety here. Data caveat that does not affect either leg: the FY2025 P&L lines are internally garbled (finance cost double-counted, EBIT 6,598 implausible) and the entire nbfc block (AUM, GNPA, NNPA, CRAR, NIM) is null, so asset quality is inferred from the residual provision line rather than observed; PAT, net worth and total assets are coherent across all four years and are all my two legs consume.

SUPRAJIT.method_1: Normalised earnings multiple: normalised EBITDA margin 11.0-12.0% on FY26 revenue 3,825 cr (vs 10.2% reported, 11.4% in FY23) less D&A 151, less interest 63.5, plus sustainable treasury income ~40 (stripping the anomalous 116 cr of FY26 other income back to what 589 cr of cash+ST investments can earn), taxed at 27% -> normalised PAT 156-207, EPS Rs 11.5-15.0. Applied 14-20x: the value-driver formula (1 - g/ROE)/(CoE - g) at ROE 12-14%, g 7-8%, CoE 12.5% justifies only 7-11x, so 14-20x already pays a franchise premium for the #1 global position in automotive control cables and the Suprajit Controls turnaround option. Range Rs 160-305.
SUPRAJIT.method_2: Sustainable free-cash-flow yield on owner earnings: normalised PAT 157-183, plus (D&A 151 - capex 118) = +33, less steady-state working-capital absorption of ~88 cr (23% of sales - the pre-FY26 intensity - applied to ~350 cr of incremental annual revenue) -> FCFE Rs 100-130 cr, capitalised at 4.5-6.5% (equivalently Gordon at CoE 12.5%, g 6-8%). Range Rs 110-215. Cross-checked against a balance-sheet anchor: justified P/B = (ROE - g)/(CoE - g) at ROE 11-15%, g 7-8%, CoE 12-12.5% gives 0.73-1.75x book of 1,437 cr = Rs 76-183/share, and EV set equal to invested capital (1,841 cr) less net debt gives Rs 87/share - both corroborate the low leg rather than the earnings leg.
SUPRAJIT.methods_are_independent: They are driven by different statements and have in fact diverged violently: FY26 PAT is 183 cr while FCF is 53 cr, a 3.5x gap. The reconciliation is entirely balance-sheet, not P&L: PAT 183 + (D&A 151 - capex 118 = +33) - working-capital absorption of ~160 cr = 56, versus reported FCF of 53. So the earnings leg is set by margin and the multiple, while the cash leg is set by working-capital intensity (Rec+Inv-Pay/sales rose 22.3% -> 26.2% over two years) and the D&A-vs-capex gap. Each can move without the other: a Suprajit Controls margin recovery lifts the earnings leg with zero effect on the cash leg unless receivables and inventory stop absorbing cash; conversely a one-time working-capital release back to 23% of sales would free ~120 cr and lift the cash leg with no change to reported EPS at all. I deliberately did NOT pair P/E with EV/EBITDA - on FY26 figures PAT is a near-mechanical function of EBITDA once D&A 151, interest 63.5 and tax are fixed, so those two would have been one method restated. The third check used (P/B against sustainable ROE) is likewise balance-sheet-driven and independent of the multiple applied to earnings.
SUPRAJIT.rationale: Leg 1 (normalised earnings, EPS Rs 11.5-15.0 at 14-20x) gives Rs 160-305; Leg 2 (FCFE Rs 100-130 cr at a 4.5-6.5% yield) gives Rs 110-215, with the P/B-vs-ROE anchor (0.73-1.75x book) at Rs 76-183 corroborating the lower leg. Key figures: revenue 3,825 cr growing 11.6% CAGR but EBIT flat at 218/220/212/238 across FY23-26 as EBITDA margin fell 11.4% -> 10.2% on acquisition dilution; OCF fell 260 -> 171 and FCF 168 -> 53 while revenue grew 39%; NOPAT ~174 on invested capital ~1,841 cr is a ROIC of only ~9.5%, at or below cost of capital, so growth here is not creating value; borrowings are now 993 cr (677 cr current) and interest rose 18 -> 64 cr; FY26 PAT of 183 is flattered by ~116 cr of other income against 3-14 cr in the three prior years, of which only ~40 cr is supportable by the 589 cr treasury book. The as-is intersection of the two legs is Rs 160-215; I widened the top to Rs 280 by giving roughly 30% weight to the Controls turnaround succeeding (EBITDA to ~520 cr, PAT to ~240 cr, worth Rs 350-420), which is a real option given the genuine #1 position in control cables but is not yet in any reported number. At Rs 504.6 the stock is 37.9x reported earnings, 19.5x EV/EBITDA, 4.8x book and a 0.8% FCF yield on a sub-cost-of-capital asset - roughly 80% above the top of my band, and every method I tried, including the most generous, topped out well below the current price.

SUPREMEIND.method_1: Normalised-earnings multiple: mid-cycle 15% EBITDA margin on FY26 revenue 11,218 cr = 1,683 EBITDA; less D&A 424, plus ~100 net non-operating income, taxed 25% -> normalised PAT ~1,050 cr, EPS ~Rs 82.7 on 12.7 cr shares. Applied 26-33x (mid-teens ROE, high-single-digit value growth, net cash, genuine but narrowing brand/distribution franchise - deliberately below the 35-45x peer band because three years of flat PAT do not support a compounder multiple). Range Rs 2,150-2,730.
SUPREMEIND.method_2: Owner-earnings / FCF-yield: FY24-26 average OCF 1,211 cr (FY26 1,215) less maintenance capex taken at 1.0-1.3x depreciation (425-550 cr, vs actual gross capex 815-890 cr) = owner earnings 665-790 cr. Capitalised at a 3.0-4.2% required cash yield, plus ~Rs 75/sh of net cash (558 cr) and part of the 762 cr investment book -> Rs 1,450-2,250. Cross-checked by explicit DCF on owner earnings (CoE 11-12%, 10-12% growth 5y, 8% next 5y, 5-6% terminal) giving Rs 1,330-2,190, which corroborates the yield-based range.
SUPREMEIND.methods_are_independent: The two legs use different numerators AND can point in opposite directions on this specific business, which is mid-capex-ramp. Leg 1 is accrual: it charges only current depreciation (424 cr) and implicitly assumes the 60% gross-block expansion (4,228 -> 6,785 cr over three years) will earn a normal return once it ramps, plus it normalises a cyclically depressed PVC-linked margin upward. Leg 2 is cash: it takes actual operating cash (1,215 cr, already after working-capital build and tax paid) and charges a maintenance-capex figure, so it is agnostic about whether the growth capex ever earns anything. The gap between the numerators is large and real - normalised PAT ~1,050 cr vs owner earnings ~730 cr, a 30% spread - and it is not arithmetic: it is the unresolved question of whether ~815 cr/yr of capex is growth capital or the cost of defending share. The evidence favours the cash leg (incremental EBIT of 195 cr on 2,557 cr of incremental gross block = ~7.6% pre-tax; ROE down from 22.5% in FY24 to 16.1%); the cyclical-PVC argument favours the earnings leg. Deliberately did NOT pair P/E with EV/EBITDA, which would have been one method restated - EBITDA 1,572 and PAT 954 are mechanically linked once D&A 424, interest 99 and 23% tax are fixed.
SUPREMEIND.rationale: Leg 1 (normalised earnings, EPS ~Rs 82.7 at 26-33x) gives Rs 2,150-2,730; Leg 2 (owner earnings 665-790 cr at a 3.0-4.2% cash yield, DCF-corroborated) gives Rs 1,450-2,250; the blended defensible band is Rs 1,850-2,600, central ~Rs 2,225. Key figures: market cap 44,011 cr (3,465.4 x 12.7 cr shares), FY26 revenue 11,218 / EBITDA 1,572 (14.0%) / PAT 954 / OCF 1,215 / capex 815 / FCF 400, net worth 6,169, net cash 558. The central judgement is that Supreme is a genuine franchise - market-leading plastic piping, net cash, 47% payout, best-in-class working capital - but it has spent three years and a 60% gross-block expansion to move PAT from 865 to 954 cr, with ROE falling from 22.5% to 16.1% and depreciation compounding faster than EBITDA, so the cash leg deserves real weight against the "cyclically depressed PVC realisations" bull case. At Rs 3,465 the stock trades at 46x trailing earnings, 7.1x book, a 1.75% owner-earnings yield and a 0.9% reported FCF yield, i.e. about 33% above the top of my band, which is a price that already assumes the capex ramp earns a franchise return it has not yet demonstrated. Upside risks I acknowledge but did not fully capitalise: a PVC realisation recovery plus anti-dumping duty could lift normalised PAT toward 1,180-1,250 cr (extending Leg 1 to ~Rs 3,070), and the associate stake carried at 762 cr book is likely worth several hundred rupees per share more at market - both are reflected in the upper half of the band rather than in a higher band.

SWARAJENG.method_1: Cycle-normalised earnings multiple: FY26 PAT Rs 196.3 cr haircut ~8% to mid-cycle Rs 180 cr (EPS Rs 147) at 17-22x, reflecting 43% ROE / 92% ROCE ex-cash and net cash, but capped by 100% revenue concentration on its 52% parent M&M's Swaraj tractor division -> Rs 2,510-3,245.
SWARAJENG.method_2: Distributable cash-flow yield: 4-yr average FCF Rs 103.4 cr scaled to a mid-cycle base (Rs 119-127 cr), capitalised at a 4.5-5.75% required FCF yield (CoE ~12%, terminal g 6-7%) plus ~Rs 180 cr net financial assets -> Rs 1,750-2,750; sustainable-dividend variant (Rs ~117 cr at 3.25-4.25% yield) gives Rs 2,255-2,950.
SWARAJENG.methods_are_independent: They are not arithmetically linked and they demonstrably disagree on this name. FY26 accrual PAT was Rs 196.3 cr while reported FCF was only Rs 46.7 cr - a 4.2x gap - because capex ran at Rs 69.8 cr against D&A of Rs 22.5 cr (gross PPE 281.6 -> 341.5) and working capital absorbed ~Rs 82 cr (receivables +31.4, other current assets +50.9). Market cap is 22.6x trailing earnings but 42.8x four-year average FCF, and the dividend (Rs 126.9 cr) exceeded FY26 FCF, funded by drawing short-term investments 180.5 -> 96.6. The earnings leg also embeds ~13% of PAT from treasury income that sits outside operating cash flow. So one leg reads a high-return compounder and the other reads a cash-thin capex ramp; their midpoints land ~24% apart (Rs 2,880 vs Rs 2,200), which is genuine tension, not one method restated. A P/E vs EV/EBITDA pairing was deliberately avoided since 13.1-13.5% EBITDA margins map almost mechanically onto the 9.4-9.9% PAT margins here.
SWARAJENG.rationale: Swaraj Engines is a captive diesel-engine supplier to Mahindra's Swaraj tractor division: Rs 2,007 cr revenue, remarkably stable 13.1-13.5% EBITDA margins across four years, 43% ROE on average equity, 92% ROCE excluding cash, Rs 112 cr net cash, and a 65% payout - a genuinely high-quality but structurally dependent business with no independent franchise, since its margin is set by the 52% shareholder that is also its only customer. Leg A (normalised EPS Rs 147 at 17-22x) gives Rs 2,510-3,245; Leg B (mid-cycle FCF Rs 119-127 cr at a 4.5-5.75% required yield, plus net financial assets) gives Rs 1,750-2,750, and a justified P/B cross-check of 6-8x on book of Rs 400.8/share gives Rs 2,405-3,206. I defend Rs 2,400-3,000, straddling the legs' narrow overlap and weighted toward the earnings leg because the FY26 cash shortfall is expansion capex at a 5.9x gross-asset turn rather than maintenance drag - but not fully toward it, because FY26 is a peak tractor year and the FCF evidence is real. At Rs 3,628.7 the stock trades 21% above my upper bound on 22.6x peak earnings and a 2.9% dividend yield that currently exceeds free cash flow, so the price already pays for the cycle and the quality: REDUCE, not AVOID.

TEGA.method_1: Normalised-earnings multiple on the operating business, cash valued separately. FY26 is a margin shock (EBITDA margin 13.7% vs 20.7-22.3% in FY23-25), so I normalise: revenue base Rs 1,700-1,800 cr at a 17-19.5% EBITDA margin (partial, not full, recovery) = EBITDA 289-351; less D&A ~100 and interest ~17, taxed at 26% = core PAT (ex cash-interest income) of Rs 130-170 cr. Multiple 26-34x, justified by ~80% recurring consumables replacement demand, a global installed base and engineering switching costs — a premium to Metso/Weir Minerals (9-15x EV/EBITDA, 20-28x P/E) for growth and India listing, but a clear discount to Indian capital-goods froth because ROIC has fallen from 16.5% to 7% and revenue growth is 3%. Operating value Rs 3,380-5,780 cr, plus net cash at 85-100% of the Rs 2,016 cr face (haircut for deployment/misallocation risk on a war chest earning ~4.6% post-tax, below CoE) = Rs 5,080-7,796 cr, i.e. Rs 676-1,038/sh on 7.51 cr shares (Rs 732-1,123 on the supplied 6.94 cr).
TEGA.method_2: Sustainable free-cash-flow capitalisation, using reported cash flow only and no margin-recovery assumption. Cumulative FY23-26 OCF Rs 976 cr less cumulative other income Rs 129 cr = Rs 847 cr of core operating cash over four years, i.e. ~Rs 212 cr/yr; maintenance capex charged at the depreciation run-rate of ~Rs 100 cr (4-yr average total capex was Rs 113 cr, so this leaves little for growth) gives sustainable core FCF of Rs 95-140 cr. Capitalised at 22-30x (3.3-4.5% FCF yield — the same quality rating as Leg 1, applied to cash rather than accrual profit so conversion is not double-penalised) = Rs 2,090-4,200 cr operating value, plus net cash Rs 1,700-2,016 cr = Rs 3,790-6,216 cr, i.e. Rs 505-828/sh on 7.51 cr shares (Rs 546-896 on 6.94 cr).
TEGA.methods_are_independent: Yes, and they disagreed materially here (Rs 676-1,038 vs Rs 505-828), which is the corroboration test doing real work rather than restating one number. Leg 1 lives entirely in the P&L: its answer is driven by whether the FY26 opex/commissioning shock reverses and the EBITDA margin returns toward 18-19%. Leg 2 never touches that assumption — it takes four years of actual cash from operations, strips out the interest income on the newly raised cash, and charges maintenance capex at the D&A run-rate. The two can diverge because Tega converts only ~55-60% of PAT into free cash: it is working-capital heavy (receivables 452 + inventory 437 = 53% of revenue) and has been spending capex above depreciation (Rs 170 cr and Rs 136 cr in FY25/26 against D&A of ~100). If margins recover but working capital keeps absorbing the growth, Leg 1 is right and Leg 2 understates; if cash conversion holds while the margin stays at 14%, Leg 2 is right and Leg 1 overstates. I deliberately avoided pairing P/E with EV/EBITDA, which would have been the same year's income statement counted twice. A third, non-primary sanity check (justified P/B on operating equity of Rs 1,391 cr at 11-13% sustainable operating ROE, CoE 13%, g 6% → 1.0-1.4x, plus cash = Rs 454-528/sh) sits below both legs, confirming my band is not skewed bearish by construction.
TEGA.rationale: Tega makes polymer/composite mill liners and mineral-processing consumables for global mining, a genuinely good recurring-replacement business, but FY26 was ugly: revenue +3.3% to Rs 1,692 cr while EBITDA fell 32% to Rs 231 cr (13.7% margin vs 20.7-22.3% in FY23-25), and core PAT stripped of cash-interest income (PBT 201 vs EBIT 136 less interest 17 implies ~Rs 82 cr other income on the newly raised cash) collapsed from ~Rs 174 cr to ~Rs 85 cr, with ROIC down to 6.9% from 16.5% two years earlier. Leg 1 (normalised core PAT Rs 130-170 cr at 26-34x, plus net cash) gives Rs 676-1,038/sh; Leg 2 (sustainable core FCF Rs 95-140 cr at 22-30x, plus net cash) gives Rs 505-828/sh, the gap being Tega's ~55-60% FCF-to-PAT conversion from heavy working capital and above-D&A capex. Note a data conflict I resolved openly: the FY26 balance sheet (equity capital 66.54 → 75.13 at Rs 10 par, reserves +2,084, financing CF +1,690) implies ~7.51 cr shares after a ~Rs 1,880 cr equity raise, not the 6.94 cr supplied, so I ran both counts and took the union of the overlap — Rs 675-890, a mid of ~782 which implies EV ~Rs 3,850 cr = 12x normalised EBITDA and 24x normalised core earnings. At Rs 1,485.5 the market is paying ~36x current EV/EBITDA and ~51x FY25 / ~78x FY26 reported PAT for a business growing 3% with halving returns on capital, and even a bullish full-margin-recovery-plus-15%-growth path does not reach it; the Rs 2,016 cr net cash is ~19% of market cap and I have already credited it near face, so the remaining gap is pure multiple. Verdict AVOID — price sits ~67% above the top of my band.

THERMAX.method_1: Normalised mid-cycle earnings multiple. Normalise PAT to Rs 850-1,050 Cr (revenue filling the doubled gross PPE base toward Rs 13,000-14,000 Cr at a 10.5-12% EBITDA margin, vs FY26 actual of Rs 10,694 Cr revenue / 10.3% margin / Rs 720 Cr PAT). Multiple 18-26x: a premium to pure project/EPC comparables (18-25x) for the technology, brand and installed-base services franchise, but capped far below the 35-50x Indian investors pay for ABB/Siemens/Cummins because those earn 20-30% ROE while Thermax earns 13.7%. Gives Rs 15,300-27,300 Cr equity = Rs 1,359-2,424/share.
THERMAX.method_2: Unlevered free-cash-flow DCF with an explicit reinvestment charge, cross-checked against a balance-sheet returns anchor. Normalised NOPAT Rs 800-950 Cr; growth 10-13% for 10-15 years fading to 5-6%; reinvestment rate set as g/ROIC using MEASURED incremental ROIC (8.9% trailing FY23-26; 15-20% if the newest capex is given a productivity lag); WACC 11-11.75% (CoE ~12.5% at Rf 6.8 + beta ~1.05 x 5.5 ERP, post-tax debt ~5.8%). Base case EV ~Rs 10,100 Cr; aggressive bull case (13% growth for 15 years at 20% ROIC) reaches ~Rs 21,000 Cr. Gives Rs 906-1,869/share. Independent cross-check: justified P/B = (ROE-g)/(CoE-g) = (13.5-6)/(12.5-6) = 1.15x book = Rs 6,380 Cr = Rs 567/share, and a 4.5-6% fair FCF yield on ~Rs 600 Cr sustainable FCF gives Rs 888-1,184/share - both harsher than the DCF, so the DCF range is already the generous end of the cash-flow family.
THERMAX.methods_are_independent: Genuinely, and they visibly disagreed. Leg 1 reads the accrual P&L and asks only "what is normalised profit worth"; Leg 2 asks two different questions the P&L cannot answer - does that profit convert to cash, and does the capital being reinvested earn its cost? For Thermax those questions have opposite answers right now. Cumulative FY23-26 PAT is +Rs 2,441 Cr while cumulative FCF is MINUS Rs 1,048 Cr, because capex ran at ~4.6x depreciation (650/844/903/952 vs D&A 117/135/159/208), gross PPE more than doubled (2,532 to 5,563), and a project business's working capital absorbed the rest; gross borrowings went 830 to 2,353 to fund it. Critically, measured incremental ROIC over the period is only 8.9% (NOPAT +Rs 291 Cr on +Rs 3,290 Cr of invested capital) against an ~11.5% WACC - so the reinvestment charge in Leg 2 destroys value where Leg 1's multiple implicitly assumes it creates value. Had capex been maintenance-only the two legs would be mechanically linked and would agree; here they landed at 1,359-2,424 vs 906-1,869 with only partial overlap, which is exactly the kind of divergence a P/E-vs-EV/EBITDA pair (both driven by the same year's EBITDA-to-PAT bridge) can never produce. I deliberately did NOT use EV/EBITDA as a second leg for that reason.
THERMAX.rationale: Leg 1 (normalised earnings, PAT Rs 850-1,050 Cr at 18-26x) gives Rs 1,359-2,424/share; Leg 2 (reinvestment-charged FCF DCF, NOPAT Rs 800-950 Cr, WACC 11-11.75%, incremental ROIC 8.9% trailing / 15-20% lag-adjusted) gives Rs 906-1,869/share, with justified P/B of 1.15x and a 4.5-6% FCF yield both pointing lower still. The central judgement is that Thermax is a real capital-goods franchise with a genuine energy-transition runway, but it is currently earning roughly its cost of capital (ROE 13.7%, post-tax ROIC ~11.7%) and has spent four years converting profit into fixed assets rather than cash, with revenue growth decelerating to 3.1% even as gross PPE doubled - so the entire investment case rests on unproven incremental returns on Rs 3,300 Cr of new capital that has so far returned 8.9%. My band of Rs 1,150-2,000 spans that uncertainty honestly: the low end is the "new capex earns 12-13%" world (still 2.3x book, a premium to a no-EVA business) and the high end sits at or above my most aggressive bull DCF. At Rs 4,306 the market pays 67x trailing PAT, ~76x EV/core-NOPAT, 44x EBITDA, 4.5x sales on a 10%-margin project business and 8.7x book on a 13.7% ROE - 2.15x my high end, hence AVOID.

TIINDIA.method_1: Normalised attributable-earnings multiple: 26-34x on normalised owner PAT of Rs 1,200-1,300 cr (reported FY26 Rs 1,116 cr; four-year PAT CAGR -1.2% despite 15.1% revenue CAGR), giving Rs 31,200-44,200 cr equity value, or Rs 1,610-2,280/share on 19.36 cr shares.
TIINDIA.method_2: Owner cash-flow value: FY26 OCF Rs 1,161 cr less maintenance capex (proxied by D&A Rs 664 cr) less incremental working capital (Rs 777 cr absorbed on Rs 3,383 cr of incremental revenue = 23% of every incremental rupee) leaves ~Rs 590 cr of steady-state distributable cash; two-stage FCFE DCF at CoE 11.5-12.5%, stage-1 growth 12-14%, terminal g 6-7.5% and terminal ROE 15-18%, plus owner share of net cash, gives Rs 890-1,415/share (capitalising the Rs 590 cr at a 4-5% yield gives Rs 610-765).
TIINDIA.methods_are_independent: Yes, and they demonstrably disagree - the ranges do not even overlap (Rs 1,610-2,280 vs Rs 890-1,415). Leg 1 keys off accrual profit and a franchise/peer multiple; leg 2 keys off what the business actually converts to cash after funding its own working capital and asset base. For TIINDIA these must diverge because reported profit is not becoming cash: capex has run at 2.2-2.5x depreciation for three straight years and working capital absorbs 23% of incremental revenue, so FCF has collapsed from Rs 991 cr (FY23) to Rs 0 (FY25) to Rs -272 cr (FY26) while PAT stayed flat. A P/E-and-EV/EBITDA "intersection" would have been arithmetic; an earnings multiple against a cash-conversion measure is a real test, and it failed, which is the signal.
TIINDIA.rationale: Consolidated revenue compounds 15.1% (Rs 14,965 cr to Rs 22,847 cr over FY23-26) but nothing reaches the owner: EBITDA margin has fallen every year (12.8% to 9.8%), the PBT-to-PAT wedge has widened from 26.7% to 39.7% (minority leakage as the listed subsidiary grows plus loss-making ventures), attributable PAT is flat at ~Rs 1,116 cr, ROE has halved from 29% to 14%, and FCF is now negative on capex of 2.2x depreciation. The earnings leg at 26-34x normalised owner PAT of Rs 1,200-1,300 cr gives Rs 1,610-2,280/share; the cash leg gives only Rs 890-1,415/share, and the non-overlap is the whole finding - the market is paying for a growth ramp and hidden stake value, not for delivered owner economics. I would defend Rs 1,350-2,050 (23-36x earnings, 3.4-5.1x book), leaning to the earnings leg because the reinvestment is real and the franchise is genuine, but refusing to underwrite 47.7x trailing earnings and 6.9x book on four years of zero EPS growth and no free cash. IMPORTANT DATA CAVEAT: the vendor share count (34.03 cr) contradicts the balance sheet - share capital is Rs 19.36 cr rising in Rs 0.01-0.03 cr ESOP increments, i.e. ~19.36 cr shares at Re 1 face value, which is the only count that produces sane multiples (P/S 2.3x vs an implausible 4.1x on a 9.8%-EBITDA-margin manufacturer); I used 19.36 cr, and if the engine uses 34.03 cr its per-share fair value will be ~43% too low for a data reason, not a methodology one. Direction is robust either way: on the vendor count the stock would be 84x earnings, i.e. dearer still.

TIMKEN.method_1: Normalised earnings multiple: mid-cycle PAT ~Rs 440 cr (trailing 415, part credit for the new capacity ramping and FY26 being a margin trough; FY25's 447 stripped of its one-off 19% tax rate) at 30-38x, a franchise premium to the ~22x market discounted for 2%/yr three-year earnings growth and a 14.4% ROE, plus Rs 305 cr net cash = Rs 1,796-2,264/share.
TIMKEN.method_2: Normalised owner free-cash-flow yield: OCF Rs 446 cr (FY26 payables-aided; 4-yr average 379) less maintenance capex at ~D&A of Rs 120 cr = normalised FCF Rs 300-340 cr, capitalised at a required entry yield of 2.5-3.5% for a net-cash 8-10% grower, plus net cash = Rs 1,180-1,849/share. Cross-checked against justified P/B = (ROE-g)/(CoE-g): at ROE 14.4%, CoE 11.7%, g 8% that is ~1.7x book versus 8.1x actual, i.e. the price embeds a sustained ~38% ROE.
TIMKEN.methods_are_independent: They are not arithmetically linked because this company is mid-capex-ramp, which is exactly where accounting earnings and owner cash flow decouple. Capex ran Rs 262/378/297 cr in FY24-26 against D&A of only Rs 85/85/106 cr (gross block +82% in three years), and working capital absorbs ~29% of sales (receivables 811 + inventory 800 - payables 610 = 1,001 cr on revenue 3,478), so reported FCF collapsed to Rs 78/10/148 cr while PAT sat flat at ~415 cr. The earnings leg is agnostic to reinvestment intensity; the cash leg prices it directly. They duly disagreed rather than corroborating: 1,796-2,264 versus 1,180-1,849, with essentially no overlap — the opposite of the P/E-versus-EV/EBITDA trap, where both legs would restate the same year's operating margin. The justified-P/B cross-check is a third, balance-sheet-based anchor keyed off ROE and cost of equity, independent of both cash flow and the earnings multiple, and it lands with the low leg.
TIMKEN.rationale: Timken India is a genuine franchise — bearings oligopoly, MNC parent technology, railway and industrial approvals, Rs 305 cr net cash, 70% EBITDA-to-OCF conversion — but the financials show a business whose earnings have stalled while its capital base ballooned: revenue compounded 7.4% (2,807 to 3,478) yet PAT went 391 to 415 over three years, EBIT margin slid 16.9% to 15.3%, and ROE fell 21% to 14.4% as gross block rose 82% on Rs 936 cr of capex versus Rs 275 cr of D&A. The earnings leg (Rs 440 cr normalised PAT at 30-38x plus net cash) gives Rs 1,796-2,264; the cash leg (Rs 300-340 cr normalised FCF at a 2.5-3.5% required yield plus net cash) gives Rs 1,180-1,849; weighting the earnings leg 60/40 because the ramp genuinely understates steady-state cash power produces a defensible band of roughly Rs 1,500-2,100. That top end is generous, not stingy: even a full-ramp bull case of Rs 5,000 cr revenue at 19% EBITDA margins (PAT ~600) by FY29 on 35x discounts back to only ~Rs 2,000 today. At Rs 3,145 the stock trades at 57x trailing PAT, 36.5x EV/EBITDA and 8.1x book — a multiple that requires a sustained ~38% ROE against a measured 14.4% — so the price sits 50-100% above my band and I would not underwrite it here despite the quality of the asset.

TITAGARH.method_1: Normalised mid-cycle earnings multiple: mid-cycle revenue ~4,200 cr at 11% EBITDA (~460 cr), less ~80 cr D&A on the enlarged post-ramp asset base and ~50 cr net financing cost, taxed at 27% = normalised PAT 230-280 cr, capitalised at 22-32x.
TITAGARH.method_2: Steady-state owner cash flow: same ~460 cr mid-cycle EBITDA less ~90 cr maintenance capex, ~55 cr cash interest and ~88 cr cash tax = ~230 cr zero-growth free cash flow, capitalised at 20-28x (3.6-5.0% FCF yield); sense-checked against the actual FY23-26 OCF record of 41 / 86 / -97 / 322 cr.
TITAGARH.methods_are_independent: They can and do move in OPPOSITE directions for this business, which is the definition of independence here. Titagarh's accrual earnings and its cash generation are decoupled by working capital: receivables run 971 cr (111 days) against a monopsony government buyer and inventory 588 cr, so roughly 30-35 paise of every incremental rupee of revenue is absorbed before any capex. When revenue grows, PAT rises and FCF falls; when revenue shrinks, PAT falls and FCF rises. FY26 is the live proof — revenue fell 17.6% to 3,186 cr, yet OCF swung from -97 cr to +322 cr. Over FY23-26 the two legs disagreed by 1,084 cr: cumulative PAT +631 cr versus cumulative FCF -453 cr. A P/E leg and an EV/EBITDA leg off the same year would have been the same arithmetic restated (PAT 121.55 is just EBITDA 283.22 less D&A 51.07 less interest 87.92 plus other income, taxed); an accrual leg against a cash-conversion leg is not, and here they land 30% apart at the midpoint (Rs 523 vs Rs 408).
TITAGARH.rationale: Titagarh is a tender-driven rolling-stock OEM selling largely into a monopsony buyer (Indian Railways) while mid-way through a metro/Vande Bharat capacity ramp: revenue went 3,853 -> 3,868 -> 3,186 cr across FY24-26, EBITDA margin oscillated 7.1-11.7%, capex ran 369 cr against 51 cr of D&A, and FY26 ROE was just 4.95% on the 2,456 cr post-QIP book (pre-tax ROCE 8.9%, below any defensible cost of capital). Leg 1 (normalised earnings) takes mid-cycle revenue ~4,200 cr at 11% EBITDA = ~460 cr, less ~80 cr D&A and ~50 cr net interest, taxed 27%, for normalised PAT of 230-280 cr; at 22-32x — already a growth multiple, capped by ~10% mid-cycle ROE against a ~12.5% CoE and by reverse-auction pricing power — that is 5,100-9,000 cr of equity, Rs 378-668/share. Leg 2 (steady-state owner cash flow) takes the same 460 cr EBITDA less ~90 cr maintenance capex, ~55 cr cash interest and ~88 cr cash tax for ~230 cr of zero-growth FCF, capitalised at 20-28x because growth here is bought rather than free, giving 3,860-7,140 cr of equity, Rs 286-529/share. The overlap is Rs 378-529, which I widen to Rs 400-580 for the genuine option value of the 35-year Vande Bharat maintenance annuity and a possible mix shift toward higher-margin passenger stock; a justified-P/B cross-check at ROE 15%, g 9%, CoE 12% gives only Rs 364, confirming the band is if anything generous. At Rs 825 the stock is 91x trailing PAT, 39.8x EV/EBITDA and 4.53x book on a business that produced -453 cr of cumulative free cash flow against +631 cr of cumulative PAT over four years — the price already discounts full execution of the FY30 bull case at a 25x exit multiple, with zero margin for the tender air-pockets that FY25 and FY26 both delivered.

TVSSRICHAK.method_1: Normalised mid-cycle earnings multiple: 4yr avg EBITDA margin 7.9% (range 6.6-9.9%) applied to FY26 revenue Rs 3,643cr at 8.0-8.75% = Rs 292-319cr EBITDA; less D&A Rs 145cr, interest Rs 48cr, tax 26% = normalised PAT Rs 73-93cr, EPS Rs 95-122 on 0.766cr shares. Multiple 12-16x (lower half of the Indian tyre peer band - below CEAT/Apollo, near JK Tyre - because normalised ROE is only 8-10%, net debt/EBITDA is 2.6x and it is the #3/#4 player in 2W/3W tyres with commodity rubber input pass-through risk). Range Rs 1,142-1,944.
TVSSRICHAK.method_2: Balance-sheet anchor: justified P/B = (ROE - g)/(CoE - g) against book of Rs 1,190cr (BVPS Rs 1,554). Sustainable ROE 9-14% (delivered 1.7-9.7% over FY23-26, avg ~6%; upper end gives credit for the just-completed capex cycle), CoE 13-14% for an illiquid leveraged small-cap cyclical, g 5-6%. Justified P/B spans 0.44x (ROE 9%) to 1.14x (ROE 14%); the defensible 0.6-1.1x = Rs 930-1,710/sh. Cross-checked against operating asset value: net fixed assets 1,095 + intangibles 104 + operating working capital 327 + investments 518 = Rs 2,045cr less net debt 739 = Rs 1,307cr = Rs 1,706/sh.
TVSSRICHAK.methods_are_independent: Leg 1 is an income-statement FLOW measure (mid-cycle margin to PAT to P/E); Leg 2 is a balance-sheet STOCK measure (net worth times a normative ROE-vs-CoE spread, cross-checked on replacement/asset value). They diverge precisely when book value grows faster than earning power, which is what happened here: gross block went 1,462 to 1,890 (+29%) and capex ran 1.25-2.4x depreciation for three straight years while PAT fell from 108 to 20 and back to 71. The earnings leg therefore says Rs 1,142-1,944 while the book leg says Rs 930-1,710 - a real disagreement of roughly 20% at both ends, not a restatement. I deliberately did NOT use EV/EBITDA alongside P/E: with D&A, interest and tax all effectively fixed here, those two are the same arithmetic wearing two hats.
TVSSRICHAK.rationale: TVS Srichakra is a sub-scale, leveraged two/three-wheeler tyre maker, not a franchise: revenue grew a modest 7% CAGR to Rs 3,643cr but EBITDA margin whipsawed 6.6-9.9% on rubber costs, PAT collapsed from Rs 108cr (FY24) to Rs 20cr (FY25) and only partly recovered to Rs 71cr (FY26), and pre-tax ROCE of 7.1% and ROE of 6.0% sit clearly below any sensible cost of capital, so the FY23-25 capex ramp (Rs 619cr against Rs 323cr of depreciation) has so far destroyed value rather than created it. The normalised-earnings leg gives Rs 1,142-1,944 and the justified-P/B leg gives Rs 930-1,710, with the operating-asset cross-check landing at Rs 1,706 - I intersect these at Rs 1,200-1,750 and would defend that mid-point of about Rs 1,475. At Rs 3,931 the stock trades at 42x trailing EPS of Rs 93, 2.5x book on a 6% ROE, and 13.3x EV/EBITDA: the price requires a 12.9% EBITDA margin or Rs 151cr of PAT, both far beyond anything achieved in four years. The genuine caveats are the tiny 0.766cr share count (a minuscule float can hold prices detached from fundamentals for a long time) and the Rs 518cr investments line whose realisability I cannot verify, but neither closes a gap of this size, so I read the current price as more than double fair value.

USHAMART.method_1: Normalised earnings multiple: 17-22x P/E on normalised PAT of ~Rs 465 cr (FY26 473, FY25 389), reflecting a genuine niche global wire-rope franchise with net cash but only ~4% revenue CAGR — premium to a commodity steel processor, well short of a franchise multiple. Gives Rs 269-349/share (11.2-14.4x EV/EBITDA equivalent).
USHAMART.method_2: Owner-earnings / FCFF DCF: NOPAT 435 cr, reinvestment rate 46% measured from realised FY24-26 capex 720 vs D&A 291 plus WC build 148, so FCFF ~240 cr; 10 yrs at the realised 7% NOPAT growth, terminal g 5% at 14% ROIC, WACC 11.0-12.5% -> equity Rs 4,600-6,250 cr = Rs 160-215/share. Cross-checked by justified P/B = (ROE 15.6% - g 6%)/(CoE 11.5-12.5% - g) = 1.5-1.9x book = Rs 166-214.
USHAMART.methods_are_independent: They can and do diverge sharply here, and the divergence is structural rather than arithmetic. The P/E leg prices accounting profit and is blind to what that profit costs to sustain; the FCFF leg charges the capex and working capital the business must actually fund and then credits only the growth that reinvestment buys. For Usha Martin those inputs point opposite ways: reinvestment absorbs ~46% of NOPAT (capex 720 cr vs D&A 291 cr over FY24-26, plus a 148 cr working-capital build on inventory 958 + receivables 643), and it bought only ~7% NOPAT CAGR because incremental return on retained equity is just 10.5% ((473-339)/(3,302-2,031)) against a 11.5-12.5% cost of equity. A pure P/E cannot see a sub-cost-of-capital reinvestment spread; the cash-flow leg is driven by almost nothing else. The result is legs that do not overlap at all (269-349 vs 160-215) — the opposite of the false-corroboration failure mode. The justified-P/B check is a supporting third read, not a co-equal leg; note it is balance-sheet based and lands with the cash-flow leg, which is why I weight that side. I deliberately did NOT pair P/E with EV/EBITDA, which here are mechanically the same statement (EBITDA 688 -> EBIT 572 -> PAT 473 with interest 20, D&A 116 and a stable 24% tax rate).
USHAMART.rationale: Usha Martin is a working-capital-heavy, mid-capex-ramp specialty wire-rope maker: revenue 3,268 -> 3,691 cr over FY23-26 (4.1% CAGR), EBITDA margin steady at 18-19% (688 cr FY26), PAT 339 -> 473 cr, net cash Rs 333 cr, ROIC ~15% and ROE 15.6%. The earnings leg at 17-22x normalised PAT of ~465 cr gives Rs 269-349; the owner-earnings FCFF leg (46% reinvestment rate, ~7% growth, WACC 11.0-12.5%) gives Rs 160-215, corroborated by a justified P/B of 1.5-1.9x on 3,302 cr book (Rs 166-214). The legs disagree because roughly half of NOPAT is consumed to buy growth at a ~10.5% incremental return, barely at or below cost of capital — real quality (top-3 global position, certification barriers in offshore/elevator rope, ~half exports, debt-free) but not value-creating compounding. I defend Rs 210-320, weighted toward the two cash/balance-sheet reads while allowing for the franchise case; even a bullish 15% PAT CAGR to FY31 at a 22x exit discounts back to only ~Rs 396. At Rs 496 (30.8x trailing, 20.7x EV/EBITDA, 4.4x book, ~2.6% normalised FCF yield) the price is ~55% above my band midpoint and requires ~9-12% perpetual growth at the measured 15% ROIC to justify — hence AVOID. Caveat flagged, not hidden: share count 29.34 cr per the feed vs share capital of Rs 30.51 cr at Re 1 face value; using 30.51 cr shifts the band to Rs 202-308, immaterial to the verdict.

VARROC.method_1: Normalised earnings multiple. Mid-cycle EBITDA margin of 9.5-9.75% on the FY26 revenue base of Rs 8,890 cr (four-year actual range 7.72-10.05%, FY26 8.92%, with gross margin on a genuine 300bp uptrend to 35.9%), less run-rate D&A ~355, interest ~120-130 post-deleveraging, tax 28% -> normalised EPS Rs 17.5-19. Applied 16-22x. Justification for that multiple: this is a tier-1 with real content-per-vehicle and EV-electronics growth, but ROIC of ~13.2% only matches a ~12.5% WACC, EBITDA margins swing 240bp year-to-year, and 2W/Bajaj customer concentration is high - so it earns neither the 30-45x quality-ancillary band (Uno Minda, Endurance) nor a 15x commodity-converter band. Range: Rs 280-420/share.
VARROC.method_2: FCFF / cash-conversion DCF. Normalised OCF ~Rs 600 cr (4-yr average 611; FY26's 537 depressed by a +Rs 353 cr swing into other current assets) less normalised capex Rs 400-430 cr (4-yr average 407, D&A ~330-350) -> FCFF Rs 180-230 cr. Two-stage on NOPAT: base NOPAT Rs 336 cr (EBIT 461 x 0.72), bull Rs 452 cr (11% EBITDA margin), grown 8% for five years at 40-45% reinvestment, terminal g 5% at 14% ROIC, WACC 12-12.5% (CoE ~13.4% on beta ~1.1, Rf 6.8%, ERP 6%; ~6% market gearing). Base equity value Rs 168/share, 11%-margin bull Rs 268/share. Corroborated by realised cash: four-year cumulative FCF of Rs 816 cr is PRE-interest (interest sits in financing CF); net of ~Rs 550 cr interest paid, cumulative FCFE is ~Rs 265 cr, or ~Rs 65 cr/year. Range: Rs 165-270/share.
VARROC.methods_are_independent: Yes, and here they actively contradict each other rather than merely being nominally distinct. Varroc is mid-capex-ramp: D&A is 42% of EBITDA and FY26 capex of Rs 469 cr is 1.41x D&A, so reported earnings and free cash flow have told opposite stories in consecutive years - FY25 PAT was Rs 70 cr while FCF was Rs 448 cr; FY26 PAT was Rs 230 cr while FCF collapsed to Rs 68 cr. That inversion is the proof of independence: the earnings leg is driven by the P&L margin and tax rate, while the cash leg is driven by capex phasing, working-capital absorption and the fact that interest is paid out of financing cash flow. Crucially I did NOT pair P/E with EV/EBITDA off the same year - that would have been one method restated, and it would have been especially misleading here because a peer EV/EBITDA multiple set by asset-lighter ancillaries systematically flatters a business that hands 42% of EBITDA straight to depreciation and reinvests more than that in capex. The two legs in fact produced NON-OVERLAPPING ranges (Rs 280-420 vs Rs 165-270), which is the substantive finding rather than a defect: the peer earnings multiple is not earned by the underlying cash economics.
VARROC.rationale: Leg 1 (normalised earnings, EPS Rs 17.5-19 at 16-22x) gives Rs 280-420; Leg 2 (FCFF DCF, NOPAT Rs 336-452 cr at 12-12.5% WACC, cross-checked against ~Rs 65 cr/yr of realised four-year average FCFE) gives Rs 165-270 - the legs do not intersect, and that gap is the whole story. Key figures: market cap Rs 10,596 cr on FY26 PAT of Rs 229.8 cr (46x trailing), EV Rs 11,256 cr on EBITDA Rs 792.7 cr (14.2x), P/B 5.95x on net worth Rs 1,780 cr, against ROIC of just 13.2% and revenue CAGR of 9.0%; the FY24 PAT of Rs 553 cr is inflated by a Rs 238 cr tax credit and should not be read as earnings power. The business is genuinely improving - gross margin up 300bp over three years, borrowings cut from Rs 1,806 cr to Rs 925 cr - but it is a thin-margin, capital-hungry, 2W-concentrated ancillary whose returns barely clear its cost of capital, so it deserves neither a franchise multiple nor the benefit of the doubt on terminal returns. I settle at Rs 290-450, weighting the earnings leg more heavily because Indian mid-caps do sustain multiples a 12.5% WACC DCF will not produce, but haircutting it toward the cash leg because four years of data show this company converts reported profit into very little cash for equity. At Rs 679 the price sits 51% above the top of my band and implicitly requires ~13% EBITDA margins (versus 8.92% delivered) AND a 25x multiple - the complete bull case realised with no discount for the possibility that it is not.
